docs.title: Two apps, one notebook
docs.text: Slate (slate-gui) is the desktop app, with menus, mouse support, a diagram canvas and a graph view. slate is the terminal app: the same editor in any terminal, over SSH too, driven entirely from the keyboard. Both read the same notes (~/.local/share/slate/notes.db) and the same config (~/.config/slate/config.toml), and you can keep both open: a note changed in one shows up in the other within a second. No accounts, no cloud.

docs.title: About the recordings
docs.text:
The animations and screenshots were recorded from the current apps on Linux in a fullscreen 1600 × 1000 workspace. The GIFs retain that resolution; tap a recording to open it full-screen and zoom in for the details.

The demo notebook has more than 25,000 notes, plus a small set of connected example notes for the graph. Most desktop recordings use Everforest Dark; the terminal recordings use Catppuccin Mocha. They are made by scripts/capture.py, so they can be recorded again whenever the apps change.

docs.title: AI: ask an agent, connect assistants
docs.text:
Slate works with AI in two directions, both off until you turn them on:

  • :ask sends a question about your note to an AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, or your own command) and lets you put the answer into the note.
  • The MCP server (slate mcp) lets AI assistants such as Claude Code, Codex or opencode search, read and edit your notes.

Slate itself has no AI model, account or API key. It uses the agent CLI you already have installed and signed in to.

docs.title: Ask an agent about your note
Setup
docs.text:
1. Install Claude Code or Codex CLI and sign in once from a terminal (claude, or codex login).
  2. Add this to ~/.config/slate/config.toml:
[agent]
enabled = true
preset = "claude"     # or "codex", or "custom" with argv = [...]
context = "note"      # what goes with your question: "selection", "note" or "none"
notes = "read"        # what the agent may do with other notes: "write", "read" or "none"

[mcp]
enabled = true        # needed for the agent to reach other notes

The settings are read on every request, so there is nothing to restart.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• :ask Which cost dominates this budget? sends the question with the note (or the selection) and shows the answer when it is ready. Agents usually take 10 to 60 seconds; you can draft your next question meanwhile.
  • Insert latest puts the answer into the note at the cursor (terminal: Enter); Copy latest copies it.
  • Ask a follow-up in the same box: the conversation continues, across notes, until you type /clear or quit.
  • Esc cancels a running request or closes the box.

With notes = "read" the agent can also look things up in your other notes ("compare this with last month's budget"); with notes = "write" it can change them too, never delete. Edits it makes to the open note arrive as one step you can undo.

What leaves your computer: your question, the note or selection (per context), and whatever notes the agent reads go to the agent's model provider. Encrypted notes are never sent: :ask is refused on them and the agent can't open them.

Details and troubleshooting: Ask the agent.

docs.title: Connect AI assistants (MCP)
docs.text:
MCP is the standard way AI assistants reach outside tools. slate mcp serves your notes to them, so you can tell your assistant "add this to my meeting notes" or "what did I write about the Lisbon trip?".

  1. Turn it on in ~/.config/slate/config.toml:
[mcp]
enabled = true
allow_delete = false   # true also lets assistants delete notes for good
  1. Connect your assistant:
claude mcp add --scope user --transport stdio slate -- slate mcp   # Claude Code
codex mcp add slate -- slate mcp                                    # Codex

For opencode or any other client, configure a stdio server that runs slate with the argument mcp.

The assistant can list and search notes (with the same search language), read them, create notes, append, replace text, rename, manage collections and archive notes. Deleting is off unless you allow it. Every change is checked against the version the assistant read, so it can't overwrite edits you made meanwhile, and an open note picks up the change within a second.

To limit a client, start its server with slate mcp --read-only (only list, search and read) or slate mcp --no-delete. Encrypted notes stay closed to every client.

Full tool list and client setup: MCP server.

docs.title: Calculations, variables and currencies
docs.text:
Every line in Slate can be a calculator. Type something that adds up and the answer appears, faintly, to the right of the line. Lines that are just text stay quiet.

RecordingScreenshot

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
200 * 1.19                 238
15% of 240                 36
sqrt(144) + 3^2            21
50 kg to lbs               approx. 110.2311310924 lbs
5 km in miles              approx. 3.1068559612 miles
3 cups to ml               709.7647095 ml

Arithmetic, percentages, powers and roots, and conversions between units of length, weight, volume, time, data and many more all work; the engine is fend. Calculations also work inside list items, checklist items and table cells. Lines that look like dates (2026-09-29) are left alone.

Keep the answer. Press Tab at the end of a line to write its result into the note (1250 * 12 becomes 1250 * 12 = 15000).

Add things up. :sum and :avg total or average the numbers in the selection (or the whole note), insert the result and copy it.

docs.title: Clock times
docs.text:
Slate understands times of day and durations, so timesheets add up:

09:10-17:30 - 45min        7h 35min
9am-5pm + 13:00-14:30      9h 30min
11:45 - 09:10              2h 35min
09:10 + 2h 30min           11:40
22:00-02:00                4h
(17:00 - 09:00) / 3        2h 40min
10:30-11:00 standup        30min

A range is two times joined by - without spaces, and runs past midnight when it needs to. Words after a calculation are a label.

docs.title: Currencies
docs.text:
Convert between currencies the same way you convert units:

RecordingScreenshot 

100 USD to EUR             approx. 90.6621601529 EUR
$10 + 5 EUR                $15.51498
2000 RSD to EUR            approx. 17.0045908229 EUR
45 GBP in JPY              approx. 9503.2658993133 JPY

Rates come from a small script you point Slate at. The repository includes one that fetches about 160 daily rates from open.er-api.com:

[currency]
argv = ["python3", "/absolute/path/to/slate/scripts/examples/rates.py", "EUR"]

The last argument is your base currency. Slate keeps the last rates on disk, so conversions work offline and right from startup; it fetches fresh rates once in the background when it starts, and again on :currency refresh. The status bar says when the rates were updated. Any program that prints rates in the same JSON shape works; see Currency rates.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Give a value a name with := and use the name anywhere in the note:

RecordingScreenshot 

nights := 3
hotel := nights * 74                 222
flights := 2 * 189.90                379.8
food := nights * 2 * 35              210
total := hotel + flights + food      811.8
total / 2                            405.9
in dollars := total EUR to USD       895.41…

Change nights to 5 and every line that depends on it updates at once.

  • Names are not case-sensitive and may contain spaces (in dollars).
  • If a name is assigned twice, the last assignment wins.
  • After three letters ([editor] variable_autocomplete_min_chars), Slate suggests matching names; Tab or Enter accepts.
  • A conversion stores its number: budget := 2000 RSD to EUR keeps the amount in euros.
  • Variable names are highlighted; in vim mode gd on a name jumps to where it is defined.
  • Variables can hold clock times and durations too: start := 09:10, lunch := 12:00-12:45, then 17:30 - start - lunch.

docs.title: Variables from other notes
docs.text:
A note can use a variable defined in another note: a link to the note, a dot, and the variable's name. Type [[, pick the note (Slate writes its id into the link and shows its title), press Esc to skip choosing a heading, then type .: Slate lists that note's variables.

RecordingScreenshot 

trips := [[01M7JWK8RMTRJ4X6RC7Y9CYH6E]].total * 3    3299.4
monthly := trips / 12                                 274.95

The other note doesn't need to be open. When its variables change, notes that use them pick up the new values. Ctrl+] follows the link to the source note and Alt+Left comes back. Away from the cursor the link reads Lisbon budget.total; because it stores the id, renaming the note never breaks it.

docs.title: Turning features off per note
docs.text:
Each note can switch calculation features on and off: :module status shows them, and :module math off (or table, variables, cross_note, style) switches one. Defaults for new notes are under [editor.modules] in the config.

The full rules are in the variables specification.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
Draw boxes, shapes and arrows right inside a note. A diagram is stored as a short block of text in the note, so it is searched, versioned, exported and synced like everything else, and the desktop app gives you a canvas to draw it with the mouse.

RecordingScreenshot

A day in the community garden: get ready, welcome the neighbours, choose an activity, and plan for the weather. The build plays at a brisk pace, then pauses on the finished plan. Tap the recording to expand it and zoom in.

docs.title: Drawing on the canvas (desktop)
docs.text:
Run :diagram to insert a new diagram and open its canvas, or click a diagram in a note to edit it.

To Do Add a shape Click or drag one from the Shapes panel, or point and press r (rectangle), o (rounded), e (ellipse), d (diamond), t (text), c (cylinder) Write a label Enter, F2 or double-click; Shift+Enter for a new line Connect two shapes Hover a shape to show its dots, drag a dot onto another shape Draw a free line Pick one from the Lines panel, or drag a dot onto empty space Move Drag (snaps to the grid and lines up with other shapes; Shift moves freely), or arrow keys Resize Drag a corner of the selected shape Bend a line Select it and drag its handles Select several Drag a box around them, or Shift+click Style The Style, Text and Arrange tabs on the right: colours, line style and width, arrows, text size and alignment, position and size Copy, paste, duplicate Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+D Undo Ctrl+Z (each gesture is one step in the note's undo) Zoom Scroll, +/-, f to fit Full screen F11 Close Esc or Close

Arrange also lines shapes up, spaces them evenly, and Create next adds a matching shape beside the selected one, already connected.

There are fifteen shapes: rectangle, rounded, ellipse, diamond, text, cylinder, callout, hexagon, clipped, triangle, actor, document, cloud, gear and arrow.

docs.title: Exporting, and editing in draw.io
docs.text:
Export… on the canvas saves the diagram as SVG or PNG (1×, 2× or 3×, on a white or transparent background), or copies a PNG to the clipboard.

An exported SVG opens for editing in draw.io (diagrams.net). The SVG carries a draw.io copy of the diagram inside it: open it with File › Open in draw.io, or name it something.drawio.svg and draw.io, its desktop app and its VS Code extension treat it as an editable diagram. Positions, labels, colours, line styles, connection points and bends carry over. A few shapes become their nearest draw.io shape (a gear becomes an ellipse), and draw.io draws curves its own way. Changes made in draw.io stay in draw.io; they don't come back into the note.

PDF export draws diagrams as pictures; Markdown export keeps their text.

docs.title: The text behind a diagram
docs.text:
Each diagram is a fenced diagram block, one line per shape or connection:

```diagram Garden day
node welcome rounded 0 40 150 60 "Welcome, neighbours!" fill=#d5e8d4
node weather rhombus 220 20 120 80 "Dry forecast?" fill=#fff2cc
node outside rounded 440 0 150 60 "Picnic outdoors" fill=#d5e8d4
node inside rounded 440 120 150 60 "In the greenhouse" fill=#e1d5e7
edge e1 welcome weather
edge e2 weather outside "Yes"
edge e3 weather inside "No" route=orthogonal
```
  • node <id> <shape> <x> <y> <width> <height> ["label"] [options]
  • edge <id> <from> <to> ["label"] [options]; an end can be a shape's id or a point @x,y
  • Options include fill=, stroke= and text= colours, dashed, dotted, stroke_width=, route=straight|orthogonal|curved, arrow=none|end|both, size=, bold, italic, align= and more; see the diagram reference.
  • Text after diagram on the opening line is a caption, shown under the picture and in PDF exports.

You can edit this text directly: in the desktop app, putting the cursor in the block shows the source with the picture under it, updating as you type. The terminal app shows the source; :diagram there inserts an empty block. In vim mode, di` with the cursor in the block clears its source and ci` clears it to type a new one; da` removes the whole block.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Any note, or a whole collection, can be locked with a password. Its text and its history are stored encrypted; without the password they cannot be read, not by Slate, not by an AI assistant, and not by anyone who copies your database.

docs.title: Encrypt one note
docs.text:
1. Open the note and run :note encrypt.
  2. Type a password, then type it again.

That's it. The note opens normally until you leave it alone: after 15 minutes without use it locks, and opening it asks for the password. In lists it shows a padlock.

  • :note encrypt on an unlocked encrypted note changes its password.
  • :note decrypt stores it unencrypted again.
  • In the desktop browser, e on a note encrypts or decrypts it.

docs.title: Encrypt a collection
docs.text:
A collection can have its own password, which protects every note in it at once. Useful for a Private or Work collection whose notes should all be locked without managing a password for each.

  1. Open the browser (Ctrl+B, desktop Standard mode Ctrl+Shift+B).
  2. Move to the collection in the collections column.
  3. Press e, then type the password twice.

What happens then:

  • Every note in the collection is encrypted with the collection's password, and so is every note that joins it later: notes created while it is your working collection, pasted into it in the browser, or added with :collection join.
  • One password unlocks them all. Opening the collection, or any note in it, asks once and unlocks every note in it.
  • Notes stay tied to the collection. While a note is in an encrypted collection it can't be decrypted on its own or given its own password; take it out of the collection (:collection leave) or decrypt the collection instead. A note that leaves keeps the collection's password until the collection is decrypted.
  • Notes that already had their own password keep it. So do notes that belong to another encrypted collection.
  • The collection can't be deleted while it still protects notes; on the desktop, deleting it first offers Decrypt….
  • To undo it, press e on the collection again and enter its password: its notes are stored unencrypted again.

docs.title: What is and isn't hidden
docs.text:
Encrypted Not encrypted The note's text The note's title (so you can find it; rename it to something vaguer, or clear the name to show "Encrypted note") Every older version in its history Its tags and collections Reminder text and attached images

Encrypted notes are left out of text search, :ask, the MCP server and the graph's links. The terminal app's window title shows only "Slate" while an encrypted note is open.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each encrypted note is sealed with AES-256-GCM using its own random key. The password doesn't encrypt the note directly; it unlocks that key (through PBKDF2 with 200,000 rounds, which is deliberately slow to make guessing expensive). That is why changing a password is instant: only the key is re-wrapped, not the note.

Keep your password safe. There is no recovery: a forgotten password means the note can't be opened.

docs.title: Encrypt everything by default
docs.text:
To make every new note encrypted, set a password in an environment variable and point Slate at it:

[editor.security]
encrypt_notes = true
password_env = "SLATE_NOTES_PASSWORD"

Markdown files opened by path (slate notes.md) can't be encrypted; they stay ordinary files.

docs.title: Export a note
docs.text:
Command Makes :export pdf ~/out/note.pdf A PDF with styled headings, lists, checklists, code, tables (with formula values), dividers, images and diagrams :export markdown [path] The note's Markdown, to a file or, without a path, the clipboard :export text [path] Plain text, to a file or the clipboard

Diagrams export as pictures in PDFs and keep their source in Markdown; see Diagrams for SVG and PNG export and draw.io. More detail: export reference.

docs.title: Back up everything
docs.text:
Command Does :backup export ~/slate-backup.zip Back up the whole notebook (notes, history, tags, collections) into one ZIP, in the background :backup export md ~/notes-md Write every note as a Markdown file, in a folder per collection :backup load <path> Restore a ZIP backup, or add notes from a Markdown folder or ZIP

Restoring a backup keeps your previous database as notes.db.before-restore, just in case. Loading a Markdown folder adds its files as notes, which is also how you bring notes in from other Markdown apps, an Obsidian vault included. A Markdown backup also opens as an Obsidian vault.

docs.title: Email into notes (IMAP)
docs.text:
Slate can pull new email into your notes, so messages you want to act on sit next to everything else. It reads mail over IMAP (with TLS) from any provider; it does not send mail.

[imap]
host = "imap.example.com"
port = 993
username = "you@example.com"
password_env = "SLATE_IMAP_PASSWORD"   # the password is read from this variable
folder = "INBOX"
auto_sync_on_startup = true            # keep checking while Slate runs
poll_seconds = 60
initial_sync_past_days = 1             # how far back the first sync looks
  • slate imap-sync checks once and exits (good for cron).
  • With auto_sync_on_startup = true, Slate checks every poll_seconds while it runs and shows a desktop notification for new mail.
  • Messages land in one inbox note per day (inbox-email-2026-11-16), newest first. Each message is imported once, never twice.

The password never goes into the config file: export it in the environment Slate starts from, for example in your shell profile:

export SLATE_IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password-here'

Many providers (Gmail, Fastmail, iCloud) need an app password for IMAP.

docs.title: Start Slate
docs.text:
To Desktop Terminal Open your last note slate-gui slate Start a new note Ctrl+N slate --new Open today's daily note :today slate today Open a Markdown file slate-gui notes/plan.md slate notes/plan.md Open a note by its id slate-gui --id <id> slate --id <id>

Slate opens on the note you had open last. A Markdown file opened by path (.md, .markdown, .mdown, .mkd) is edited in place and saved back to the same file; it does not go into the database.

docs.title: Your first note
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+N and start typing. The first line becomes the note's title (start it with a letter and the desktop app makes it a # heading for you). There is no save button: Slate saves a moment after you stop typing, and again whenever you switch notes or quit. Ctrl+S saves right away.

An empty note shows a short cheat sheet of what you can write until you type the first key.

docs.title: Find your way around
docs.text:
A few keys get you almost everywhere:

Key What it opens Ctrl+P The note switcher: type part of a title, then Enter twice to jump to the best match Ctrl+N A new note Ctrl+E The command bar (: does the same in vim's Normal mode) Ctrl+B The browser: collections, notes and a preview (desktop Standard mode: Ctrl+Shift+B) F1 Help: every shortcut with how it works, then every command Ctrl+Shift+P The command palette (desktop) F4 Information about the open note Ctrl+Q Quit

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Most of Slate is reachable through commands. Press Ctrl+E, type a few letters, and suggestions appear: exp offers export, then its formats. Tab or Down picks a suggestion, Enter runs it. Commands you used recently come first. Mistype one and Slate suggests the closest (:colection → did you mean :collection?).

F1 opens help. On the desktop it is organized by topic (getting started, moving around, editing, search, macros, links, tables, calculations, commands, keyboard shortcuts); type to filter it. In both apps, Enter on a command in help puts it in the command bar for you.

docs.title: Two editing modes
docs.text:
The desktop app has two editing modes, switched in View › Editing mode:

  • Standard works like any other editor: Shift+arrows select, Ctrl+Home/Ctrl+End go to the start or end of the note, Ctrl+C/X/V copy, cut and paste, Ctrl+B/Ctrl+I make text bold or italic, Ctrl+Z undoes.
  • Vim is modal editing with motions, operators, text objects, registers, macros and . repeat. See Vim mode, macros and scripts.

The terminal app is always modal, but it starts in Insert mode so you can just type; Esc takes you to Normal mode. Set [editor] vim_mode = true to start in Normal mode instead.

docs.title: Where your notes live
docs.text:
What Where (Linux) Notes, tags, collections, history ~/.local/share/slate/notes.db (SQLite) Desktop window and view settings ~/.local/share/slate/gui-settings.json Configuration ~/.config/slate/config.toml

The config file is created on first run with every setting listed. See Themes and configuration.

docs.title: Linking notes
docs.text:
Type [[ and a note picker opens. Type part of a title, then Tab or Enter to pick a note. Slate then offers that note's headings; pick one to link straight to it, or press Esc to link the whole note.

Away from the cursor a link shows the note's title, underlined. Underneath it stores the note's id ([[01M7JWK8RMTRJ4X6RC7Y9CYH6E]]), so renaming the other note never breaks the link.

Key Does [[ Insert a link and open the note picker Ctrl+] (vim also gd) Follow the link at the cursor Alt+Left / Alt+Right (desktop) Back and forward through the notes you visited K (vim Normal) Preview the linked note in a popup Ctrl+K (desktop Standard mode) Insert a link

A link can carry a heading and its own label: [[id#Heading]], [[id|label]], [[id#Heading|label]]. A link to a note that no longer exists shows (no such note) and comes back to life if the note does.

Links also carry values: [[id]].total uses the variable total from the linked note (see Variables from other notes).

Ordinary web links, [text](https://…), are styled too.

docs.title: The graph
docs.text:
:graph (desktop: File › Note graph…) draws your notes as dots and their links as lines, starting from the open note and the notes within two links of it, in both directions.

RecordingScreenshot

The recording follows 26 example notes inside the larger demo notebook. Writing, research, numbers, design and projects each have their own color group. Selecting a note highlights its connections.

Key Does Arrow keys or h j k l Select the nearest note in that direction Tab / Shift+Tab Step through all notes Enter, double-click Open the selected note c or Space Recentre on the selected note + / - More or fewer link hops (1 to 4) w Switch between the local graph and every note / (desktop also Ctrl+F) Find notes in the graph by title; n / N step through matches Scroll, drag (desktop) Zoom, pan, or drag a note around Esc Close the graph

On the desktop, hovering or selecting a note brightens it and its neighbours while everything else fades. f or the gear button opens Filters:

  • Filter hides notes that don't match a search query (same syntax as the note switcher), for example #topic/sailing -#status/draft.
  • Orphans and Existing notes only hide unlinked notes and links to missing notes.
  • Groups color the notes matching a query, each in its own circle, so a topic or tag stands out. Click a group's swatch to pick its color.
  • Display adds arrows, and scales dots, lines and labels.

Filters, groups and display options are remembered.

Color groups can use the same queries as search. Here, each collection gets its own region, making related notes easy to spot.

In the terminal the graph is drawn with characters: ◆ is the centre note, ◉ the selection and ○ a link to a missing note. ] and [ zoom, Shift+H/J/K/L pan, and 0 shows the whole graph again.

The first time you open the graph Slate reads every note's links once ("Indexing links…"); after that only notes you changed are read again, so it opens at once.

docs.title: Organizing
docs.text:
Slate gives you three ways to arrange notes, and they combine freely:

  • Collections are like folders, except a note can be in several.
  • Tags label notes across collections (meeting, idea, topic/sailing).
  • Pins keep favourites at the top of every list.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Command Does :collection create Work Create a collection :collection choose Work (or Ctrl+G) Make it the working collection :collection choose none Back to all notes :collection join Work / leave Work Add the open note to it / take it out :collection update Work Rename it, describe it, set default tags for new notes :collection delete Work Delete the collection, keeping its notes :collection purge Work Delete the collection and its notes

The working collection is where new notes go, and the note switcher looks there first (Ctrl+L switches to all notes). Set [startup] default_collection = "Work" to start in one.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: :tag add work and :tag remove work change the open note's tags. :organize (or clicking the tags on the desktop) opens a dialog listing the note's tags and collections first, then all the others; type to find or create one, Enter adds or removes it. Tags are separate from the note's text, so adding one never changes what you wrote.

docs.title: Pins
docs.text: :note pin pins the open note; P in the browser pins a note or collection. Pinned items come first in the browser and pickers.

docs.title: The browser
docs.text:
Ctrl+B (desktop Standard mode: Ctrl+Shift+B) opens a three-column browser, like a file manager: collections, the notes in the open collection, and a live preview.

RecordingScreenshot

Key Does type Filter note titles (the filter has focus when it opens) Esc Leave the filter to move around j/k, arrows Move Tab (desktop), h/l Between the collections and the notes Enter, o Open the note or collection Ctrl+F Search the text of the notes in this collection t / T Edit the note's tags / filter by tags Space, Ctrl+A Select notes y then p Add the selected notes to another collection x then p Move them there d Take them out of this collection (they stay in your notes) D Delete them (asks first) u Undo the last paste or removal n / r New note / rename e Encrypt or decrypt a collection or note (see Encryption) H The note's history s Sort by date or title a or ? All actions for what is selected

Unsorted lists notes in no collection. Lists load in pages as you scroll, so the browser opens instantly even with tens of thousands of notes.

docs.title: Note history
docs.text:
Slate keeps older versions of every note, automatically. Edits a few minutes apart count as one session, and each session keeps the text from before it. Versions store only the lines that changed, so even large notes cost little. Old versions thin out over time: everything from the last day, then one per day for a month, then one per week.

RecordingScreenshot

Open it with :history, H in the browser or Ctrl+R in the note switcher. Pick a version to see what restoring it would change (split or unified on the desktop), Tab shows the version's text, and Enter restores it after asking. Restoring is itself kept as a version, so nothing is ever lost.

docs.title: Note info
docs.text: F4 or :info shows the open note's title, id, tags, collections, when it was created and last saved, and whether it is encrypted.

docs.title: Daily notes and quick capture
docs.text:
:today (or slate today from a shell) opens today's note, creating it from a template. From the shell you can drop a line into it without opening Slate, which works well with scripts, cron jobs and key bindings:

RecordingScreenshot 

slate capture call the bank about the card     # adds "- 20:37 call the bank…"
echo "deploy 4.2 finished" | slate capture     # captures piped text
make test 2>&1 | slate append                  # appends output to the last edited note
make test 2>&1 | slate append --id <note-id>   # …or to a given note
slate --list                                   # list notes

The daily note's id prefix and template are set under [daily]:

[daily]
note_prefix = "daily"
template = "# {date}\n\n"

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Slate is built to open instantly and stay quick no matter how big your notes or your notebook get. Every recording in this guide runs on a demo notebook that is far larger than most people's:

  • 25,000 notes in a 4 GB database,
  • the largest single note 6.3 MB, almost 800,000 words (70,000 lines),
  • 130,000 links between notes.

With all of that, Slate opens on the last note, finds any note by title as you type, searches the text of every note, opens the 6 MB note and scrolls it, searches inside it, and draws the graph of all 25,000 notes. See the tour, search and graph recordings.

docs.title: How it stays fast
docs.text:
• Nothing heavy blocks your typing. Saving, searching, exchange-rate updates, backups, reading linked notes and laying out the graph all run in the background. A small spinner in the status bar shows work that lasts longer than a second.
  • Only what you see is worked on. In large notes, calculations are computed for the visible part first and the rest fills in off to the side. Styling is computed once per change, not on every frame.
  • Small changes stay small. An edit updates only the lines it touches; history stores only changed lines; the link index rereads only notes that changed since last time.
  • Lists load in pages. The switcher, browser and pickers fetch 100 notes at a time as you scroll, so they open at once with any number of notes, while title filters still search everything in the background.
  • Search uses an index. Text search goes through SQLite's full-text index instead of reading every note.
  • The graph scales. Big graphs are split into communities and laid out on a background thread; when tens of thousands of notes are on screen, the desktop draws the most connected ones and adds detail as you zoom in.
  • Native, not a web page. The desktop app draws with the GPU (no browser engine inside), and the terminal app is a single small binary, so both use little memory.

docs.title: If something feels slow
docs.text:
:perf on starts recording timings, :perf dump writes the slowest operations to a log, and :perf where shows where the log is. Attach that log to a bug report and it tells exactly what was slow.

For the measurements and the benchmarks behind these claims, see the performance reference.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Slate has one search language, used everywhere you look for notes, plus a quick find inside the open note.

Where Key Searches Note switcher Ctrl+P Titles, tags, collections and text of all notes Find in note Ctrl+F (vim: /) The open note Browser filter and text search Ctrl+B, then type / Ctrl+F Titles, or text within a collection Sidebar search (desktop) Ctrl+Shift+F Titles and text Graph find and filter /, f in the graph Notes in the graph Heading picker :toc Headings of the open note Web lookup :lookup The web

docs.title: The note switcher
docs.text:
Ctrl+P, type a few letters, then Enter twice: the first moves from the search box to the results with the best match picked, the second opens it (or use Down/Up to pick another first). Plain words match titles fuzzily and in order: photo 116 finds Photometry project 11681. The switcher shows each note's collections and tags, and the best match comes first.

RecordingScreenshot

Add fields to narrow it down:

Write Finds notes title:"daily log" Whose title contains the phrase #work or tag:work Tagged work coll:Work or collection:"Work notes" In that collection contains:"release date" or text: Whose text contains the phrase -#draft, NOT title:old Without the tag, or not matching (#work OR #home) AND -title:draft Combinations; AND binds tighter than OR

Typing #, tag: or coll: opens suggestions right away; Tab accepts one and the desktop shows it as a pill. Text searches show the matching line under each note with the words highlighted, and opening the note puts the cursor on that line.

The query in the recording, #topic/sailing contains:mooring -#status/draft, finds sailing notes that mention mooring and are not drafts.

In the search box, Up and Down bring back earlier searches. In the results, Up from the first row, Tab or Esc go back to the search box, and typing edits the query again.

More switcher keys: Ctrl+L switches between the working collection and all notes, Ctrl+N creates a note, Ctrl+R opens the selected note's history and Delete deletes it (after asking).

docs.title: Find in the note
docs.text: Ctrl+F (vim: /) searches the open note as you type and highlights every match. Tab/Down and Shift+Tab/Up step through them, Enter keeps your place (vim: then n/N), and Esc takes you back to where you started. It is fast even in huge notes; in the opening tour it searches a note of almost 800,000 words.

docs.title: Search inside a collection
docs.text: In the browser (Ctrl+B), typing filters titles, and Ctrl+F searches the text of the notes in the open collection. Results show the matching line, and the preview scrolls to it with the words highlighted. See the browser.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Encrypted notes are found by title, tags and collection, never by their text.
  • Operator words work in lowercase too (and, or, not).
  • Quotes keep spaces in a value: title:"weekend in lisbon".
  • [search] beautiful = false shows queries as plain text, without pills and dimmed field names.

docs.title: Web lookup
docs.text: :lookup rust ownership searches the web without leaving Slate. Enter opens a result in your browser; Shift+Enter inserts it into the note as a Markdown link. It uses DuckDuckGo by default; Brave or Google can be set under [web_search] with an API key.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables are ordinary Markdown tables that keep themselves tidy: columns line up as you type, numbers align right when the column says so, and cells can hold formulas like a small spreadsheet.

RecordingScreenshot

docs.title: Making a table
docs.text:
• Desktop: Ctrl+Shift+T (or Insert table in the right-click menu) inserts an empty table. Typing | in the desktop app writes a literal |, so tables are made this way rather than by typing pipes.
  • Terminal: type the header row with pipes (| Item | Qty |); | starts a row or adds a column.
  • Paste from a spreadsheet: copy cells from a spreadsheet (tab-separated) or CSV text and paste outside a table; Slate turns them into a table whose first row is the header (on an empty line, or below the cursor's line).
  • Or paste or type Markdown table text: | --- | under the first row makes it the header, and ---: aligns a column to the right.

docs.title: Moving around
docs.text:
Key Does Tab / Shift+Tab Next / previous cell; Tab in the last cell adds a row Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right Previous / next cell Up / Down Same column, row above / below Enter (desktop) Same cell one row down, adding a row after the last Ctrl+Enter (desktop) New empty row below; on the last row, leave the table Shift+Enter A line break inside the cell

Shift+arrows select a rectangle of whole cells in both apps: copying gives tab-separated text (Ctrl+C, or y in the terminal's Normal mode), Delete clears them, and Ctrl+D / Ctrl+R fill them (see Filling cells). On the desktop you can also click a cell to edit it, and hovering a table's right or bottom edge shows a + strip that adds a column or a row. Wide tables scroll sideways instead of wrapping. In vim mode, ci|, di| and yi| change, delete and copy a cell.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
A cell that starts with := is a formula. The table shows its value; the formula appears only while the cursor is in the cell.

Formula Means :=(1,2) * (1,3) Data row 1, column 2 times data row 1, column 3 :=(.,2) * (.,3) Columns 2 and 3 of the formula's own row :=(.-1,.) + (.,4) The cell above plus column 4 of this row: a running total :=(.,2) * ($1,$4) $ pins a number, so filling never moves it :=sum_col(), :=avg_col() Sum / average of the other numbers in this column :=sum_row(), :=avg_row() Sum / average of the other numbers in this row :=tax_rate * (2,4) Note variables work in formulas too

References are (row, column), counting data rows from 1 (the header is not a row). A . stands for the formula's own row or column, optionally with an offset such as .-1. Typing sum or avg_ in a formula cell offers the helpers. Errors show in the cell: !ERROR#out_of_bounds, !ERROR#non_numeric, !ERROR#self_reference and !ERROR#cycle.

Here is the table from the recording as it is stored:

| Item      | Qty | Price |         Total |
| --------- | --: | ----: | ------------: |
| Tram pass |   2 |  6.60 | :=(1,2)*(1,3) |
| Museum    |   2 |    12 | :=(2,2)*(2,3) |
| Dinner    |   3 | 28.50 | :=(3,2)*(3,3) |
| Sum       |     |       |   :=sum_col() |

To total some rows by hand, select them and run :sum or :avg.

docs.title: Filling cells
docs.text:
Write a formula or a date once and fill it into the cells next to it, as in a spreadsheet.

RecordingScreenshot

  • Drag the handle (desktop): the focused cell shows a dot where its right and bottom borders meet. Drag it down or up the column, or along the row, and release. Dragging past the top or bottom of the window scrolls the note; the fill stops at the table's first and last rows, never the header. Esc while dragging cancels.
  • Keys (both apps): select cells with Shift+arrows, starting at the cell to copy, and press Ctrl+D to fill down or Ctrl+R to fill right.

A fill is one undo step. What each copy gets:

In the source cell Each filled cell gets :=(2,2)-(1,2) References moved by the copy's distance: one row down reads :=(3,2)-(2,2) :=(.,2) * (.,3) The same text: . already means "this row" :=(.,2) * ($1,$4) $1,$4 kept, so every row reads the same rate cell 03. November 2026. The next day, in the same format: 04. November 2026. 455801, N/A A plain copy

Dates are recognised as 2026-11-03, 3.11.2026., 03. 11. 2026, 03. November 2026., 3 Nov 2026 and November 3, 2026, and keep their dots, zero padding and month spelling. Slash dates such as 11/03/2026 are copied as they are, since the day and month order is ambiguous. A reference moved above the first row reads !ERROR#out_of_bounds.

docs.title: The terminal app
docs.text:
slate is the whole of Slate in a terminal: the same notes, the same editor, calculations, tables, links, search, browser, history, graph, encryption and AI features, driven entirely from the keyboard. It is a single small binary, starts instantly, and works over SSH.

RecordingScreenshot

docs.title: Getting around
docs.text:
Key Does Ctrl+P Note switcher (the same search language) Ctrl+B, or - in Normal mode Browser: collections, notes and a preview, like the yazi file manager Ctrl+G Choose the working collection Ctrl+E, or : in Normal mode Command bar, with word completion (Tab picks, Up recalls history) F1, or ? in Normal mode Help F4 Note info Ctrl+Q Quit

The app starts in Insert mode, so you can type straight away; Esc switches to vim's Normal mode (see Vim mode). The status bar shows hints for the main keys ([editor] status_hints = false hides them), and while text is selected it shows the sum, average and count of the numbers in it.

docs.title: What differs from the desktop app
docs.text:
• Diagrams show their source text. :diagram inserts an empty diagram block; draw it in the desktop app.
  • Images show as [image: …]. gx previews one inside the terminal with sixel, kitty or iTerm2 graphics when your terminal supports them ([terminal] images), with a block-character fallback; o opens it in your image viewer, and gX skips the preview.
  • The graph is drawn with characters; ]/[ zoom and Shift+H/J/K/L pan.
  • Tables are edited as text, with cell-aware keys. Shift+arrows select whole cells, which Ctrl+D / Ctrl+R fill and y copies; there is no fill handle to drag (see Filling cells).
  • Fonts come from your terminal's settings. Icons use a Nerd Font by default; set [theme] icons = "unicode" or "ascii" otherwise.

docs.title: Colours and clipboard
docs.text: Slate detects whether your terminal supports true colour, 256 colours or 16, including over SSH and inside tmux, and honors NO_COLOR. Copies go to the system clipboard through wl-copy, xclip, xsel, pbcopy, tmux or the terminal itself (OSC 52). Set [terminal] clipboard = "osc52" to always copy through the terminal, which works over SSH.

docs.title: From the shell
docs.text:
slate                      # open the last note
slate --new                # start a new note
slate notes/plan.md        # edit a Markdown file in place
slate today                # today's daily note
slate capture buy milk     # add a line to today's note without opening Slate
cmd | slate append         # append output to the last edited note
slate --list               # list notes
slate imap-sync            # pull new email once
slate mcp                  # serve notes to AI assistants
slate run <script>         # run one of your scripts on stdin

See Organizing for capture and append, and AI for slate mcp.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Desktop: View › Theme switches instantly and is remembered. It offers Everforest Dark (the default) and Light, neutral Default Dark and Light, the 14 color schemes below, and From config, which follows the [theme] section of the config file like the terminal app does.

Terminal: set the scheme in the config file; changes apply live, without a restart:

[theme]
color_scheme = "catppuccin-mocha"
accent = "auto"        # or amber, sage, rose, plum, cobalt, slate, or "#4f7bd9"
icons = "nerd"         # "unicode" or "ascii" if your font has no Nerd Font icons

The color schemes: slate-light, slate-dark, catppuccin-mocha, catppuccin-latte, gruvbox-dark, gruvbox-light (the terminal default), dracula, dark, white, solarized-dark, solarized-light, nord, tokyo-night and one-dark.

Your own colours. [theme.colors] overrides single colours with hex values. background = "none" lets the terminal's own background (and its transparency) show through:

[theme.colors]
background = "none"
accent = "88c0d0"
code-block-background = "3b4252"
variable = "ebcb8b"

Keys: foreground, background, accent, code-block-background, selection-background, keyword, string, number, comment, function, type, variable, search-match, search-current.

docs.title: Desktop look and feel
docs.text:
Setting Where Font and size [theme] font = "JetBrains Mono", font_size = 16, fallback = [...] Note text size Ctrl+=, Ctrl+-, Ctrl+0 resets (View › Zoom in/out, remembered) Interface text size View › Interface text (85% to 150%) Proportional prose View › Proportional prose: text in a sans face, code and tables stay monospace Line wrapping View › Wrap lines (Alt+Z) Line numbers View › Line numbers, or [editor] line_numbers Sidebar Ctrl+\ Distraction-free preview F11 (Esc leaves) Animations [gui] animations = false, or [gui.dialog_animation] style = "none", "fade", "slide", "fade-slide" or "bounce"

The window reopens at the size and place it closed with.

docs.title: The config file
docs.text:
~/.config/slate/config.toml (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/slate/config.toml) is created on first run with every setting and a comment for each. Both apps read it. The settings people change most:

[editor]
autosave = true                  # save after a short pause
vim_mode = false                 # start in vim Normal mode
wrap = true                      # soft-wrap long lines (tables and code scroll instead)
checklist_auto_reorder = true    # ticked items sink to the bottom
format_on_save = false           # tidy Markdown before each save
date_format = "%Y-%m-%d"
date_time_format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"
variable_autocomplete_min_chars = 3
command_popup = true             # desktop: suggestions above the command bar

[editor.modules]                 # calculation features for new notes
math = true
table = true
variables = true
style = true
cross_note = true

[startup]
default_collection = ""          # start in this collection

[daily]
template = "# {date}\n\n"

[search]
beautiful = true                 # pills and dimmed field names in search boxes

[terminal]
images = "auto"                  # sixel, kitty, iterm2, halfblocks or off
clipboard = "auto"               # "osc52" keeps copies in the terminal (works over SSH)

Other sections are covered on their own pages: [currency] (calculations), [imap] (email), [agent] and [mcp] (AI), [editor.security] (encryption), [scripts] and [keybindings] (scripts), [web_search] (lookup).

Every setting is described in the configuration reference.

docs.title: Vim mode, macros and scripts
docs.text: This page is for people who like to keep their hands on the keyboard. If you know Vim you already know most of it; if you don't, you can skip it and never miss anything.

docs.title: Turning vim mode on
docs.text:
• Terminal: the app is always modal. It starts in Insert mode so you can type; Esc goes to Normal mode. [editor] vim_mode = true starts in Normal mode.
  • Desktop: View › Editing mode › Vim. The status bar shows the mode in color: accent for Normal, blue for Insert, purple for Visual.

The vim engine is shared by both apps, so the keys behave the same in each.

docs.title: Moving and editing
docs.text:
Keys Does h j k l, w b e, 0 ^ $ Move by character, word, line gg, G, 12G First line, last line, line 12 f, t) F( T", then ; , Jump to a character on the line, and repeat % Matching bracket gj / gk Down / up one screen row on wrapped lines i a I A o O Insert before, after, at line start, at line end, new line below, above x, r{c}, s, S, D, C, J Delete, replace, substitute, delete or change to line end, join dd, yy, cc, 3dd Delete, copy, change lines d c y + any motion dw, c$, y%, df,, ct) … p / P Paste after / before (from the system clipboard when the register is empty) u / Ctrl+R Undo / redo . Repeat the last change, including what you typed v, V Visual and visual-line selection; then d y c, or : for a command on the selection

Text objects work with d, c and y: iw/aw (word), i( i[ i{ i" i` i* i~ i_ and their a forms (inside or around delimiters, including Markdown emphasis), and i|/a| for a table cell.

Slate extras in Normal mode:

Keys Does gd Follow a link, or jump to a variable's definition K Preview the linked note gx Preview the image at the cursor gX Open the image at the cursor in your image viewer di` / ci` In a fenced block such as a diagram: clear its body (ci` leaves an empty line to type in); da` removes the whole block za Fold or unfold - Open the browser /, then n / N Search the note ? All keys, with how each works

After a prefix like d, c, g or ci, the status bar lists the keys that can follow and what each does, so you never have to remember them all.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Record a sequence of keys once and replay it:

Keys Does qa Start recording into register a (any of a–z, 0–9) q Stop @a Replay it 5@a Replay it five times

In the recording above, qa I- [ ] <Esc> j q turns one line into a checklist item, and 3@a does the next three.

docs.title: Your own key bindings
docs.text:
Bind keys to any Slate command in ~/.config/slate/config.toml:

[keybindings.normal]
"<Space>t" = "today"
"<Space>g" = "graph"
"<Space>e" = "export pdf /tmp/note.pdf"

[keybindings.editor]          # Insert mode, or the desktop's Standard mode
"<C-t>" = "date"

[keybindings.visual]
"<C-b>" = "bold"

Keys are written like <C-x> (Ctrl), <Space>, <Esc>, <Enter>, <Tab>, arrows and plain characters; a binding is up to 8 keys. Restart Slate after changing them.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Hook your own programs into Slate: a script gets the selection, the note or nothing on stdin, and its output replaces the selection, is inserted, or is shown as a message.

[scripts.uppercase]
argv = ["python3", "/home/you/slate-scripts/uppercase.py"]
input = "selection"            # "none", "selection" or "note"
output = "replace-selection"   # "insert", "replace-selection" or "message"

[keybindings.visual]
"<C-u>" = "run uppercase"

Run one with :run uppercase (arguments follow the name). Ready-made examples are in scripts/examples; the full protocol is in Scripts and shortcuts. Scripts also run from the shell: echo hello | slate run uppercase.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
Slate notes are plain Markdown. There is no separate preview: headings, emphasis, lists and the rest are styled right where you type them, and the raw Markdown shows again on the line you are editing.

RecordingScreenshot

docs.title: Markdown as you type
docs.text:
You type You get # Title, ## Section, ### … Headings (levels 1–6) **bold**, *italic*, ~~strike~~, `code` Inline styles - item, 1. item Bullet and numbered lists - [ ] task A checklist item; - [x] is ticked > quote A quote, drawn with a rail beside it ``` A code block, drawn as one rounded surface ---, *** or ___ alone on a line A divider across the page [text](https://…) A link [[ A link to another note (see Links)

Lists continue themselves. Enter on a list item starts the next one, numbered lists count up, and Enter on an empty item ends the list. Tab and Shift+Tab indent and outdent an item.

Checklists. Type /x at the end of an item to tick it, or use :checklist toggle (desktop Standard mode: Ctrl+Enter). With [editor] checklist_auto_reorder = true, ticked items move below the open ones, as in the recording above.

docs.title: Formatting from the keyboard
docs.text:
Select text, then run a format command, or on the desktop use the small toolbar that appears over a selection.

Command Desktop shortcut (Standard mode) Does :bold, :italic, :strike, :icode Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+Shift+X Toggle an inline style :h1, :h2, :h3, :format text Ctrl+Alt+1/2/3, Ctrl+Alt+0 Headings, or back to plain text :ulist, :olist, :checklist Ctrl+Shift+8/7/9 Turn lines into a list :format clear Remove inline styles :format Tidy the whole note's Markdown

[editor] format_on_save = true runs :format before every save.

The selection toolbar also shows the sum of the numbers you selected, and the terminal status bar shows sum, average and count while text is selected.

docs.title: Undo and history
docs.text: Ctrl+Z undoes and Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z) redoes; in vim mode u and Ctrl+R do the same. Undo puts the cursor back where the change happened. Beyond undo, Slate keeps older versions of every note; see Note history.

docs.title: Folding and outline
docs.text:
• :fold, :unfold, :fold-toggle (vim: za, zc, zo) fold the section, list or block at the cursor. On the desktop, click the arrow beside a line number. A folded block shows how many lines it hides.
  • :toc opens a heading picker for the note: type to filter, Enter jumps.
  • :toc insert writes a table of contents into the note; :toc refresh updates it after you change headings.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
![alt text](./assets/photo.png) shows the image. On the desktop a line with only an image is drawn as the picture; gx on it or Ctrl+click on the picture shows it fitted to the window, and right-click → Copy image puts the full-size original on the clipboard. In the terminal it shows as [image: alt text]; gx previews it in the terminal (sixel, kitty or iTerm2 graphics, with a fallback). In both, o in the preview opens the image in your image viewer, and gX opens it there directly.

To add one, paste an image file path, or paste a screenshot from the clipboard: Ctrl+V on the desktop, p or :paste-image in the terminal. The image is copied into the note's assets. Remote images are never fetched.

docs.title: Dates and reminders
docs.text:
• :date opens a date picker and inserts the date. Type tomorrow, next friday 10 pm or in 3 weeks, or pick it on the calendar.
  • :remind sets a reminder on the current line. It shows beside the line and pops up a desktop notification when it is due. :remind toggle removes it.
  • Dates use [editor] date_format and date_time_format from the config.

docs.title: Clipboard
docs.text: Yanks and copies go to the system clipboard. :clip-watch on pastes everything you copy elsewhere into the note, one entry after another, until :clip-watch off. Handy for collecting quotes or links while browsing.

docs.title: Changes made elsewhere
docs.text: If the open note changes outside Slate (in the other app, through an AI assistant, or from slate capture), Slate loads the new text within a second as one step you can undo. If you have unsaved edits it keeps yours and tells you: :w! keeps your version, :e! loads the other one.

docs.title: Ask the Agent (:ask)
docs.text:
:ask <prompt> sends a question to the agent CLI you already have (Claude Code, Codex, or your own command) and shows its answer. The desktop app keeps a follow-up input below the scrollable conversation; Enter sends the prompt, and Insert latest inserts the latest answer at the cursor. In the terminal app, Enter inserts the answer from the result view. Ask keeps one conversation across notes until you clear it. With note access on, the agent can also read your other notes and edit notes through Slate's MCP server. It is off by default in both desktop and terminal apps.

  • Setup
  • Using it
  • What is sent, and what the agent can reach
  • Edits the agent makes
  • Custom agents
  • Limits

docs.title: 1. Install and sign in to an agent CLI
docs.text:
Install Claude Code or Codex CLI using the vendor's instructions for your OS. Installing a desktop agent app alone does not necessarily install its CLI. In a terminal, verify the executable you intend Slate to use:

claude --version
# or
codex --version

Run claude and complete sign-in (use /login inside Claude Code if needed), or run codex login for Codex authentication. Finish authentication before invoking Ask: Slate's background worker cannot answer an interactive login prompt. Slate does not have its own API-key or model configuration. Built-in presets use the CLI's default model and authentication; they deliberately suppress user settings/configuration as described below.

docs.title: 2. Locate Slate's config
docs.text:
Edit the existing config.toml; merge the examples into its [agent] and [mcp] sections rather than adding duplicate sections.

OS Config path Linux $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/slate/config.toml, default ~/.config/slate/config.toml macOS ~/Library/Application Support/io.github.slate/config.toml Windows %APPDATA%\github\slate\config\config.toml

These are native Slate paths. Slate running inside WSL uses the Linux path. The complete defaults are in config.example.toml.

docs.title: 3. Choose the agent and note access
docs.text:
[agent]
enabled = true
preset = "claude"       # "claude", "codex", or "custom"
context = "selection"   # "selection", "note", or "none"
notes = "read"          # "write", "read", or "none"
timeout_seconds = 300  # 1..3600

[mcp]
enabled = true         # Required for Slate note tools
allow_delete = false   # Ask never gets delete_note, even when this is true

To switch to Codex, change only preset = "codex". Do not add argv to a built-in preset; it is accepted only for preset = "custom" (see below). Unknown settings, invalid enum values, and invalid combinations are errors. There is no separate Slate model selector or extra-arguments setting for presets.

context selects what is attached from the current note on each turn. notes controls the agent's MCP access to the note database. They are independent: context = "note", notes = "none" sends the current note without starting a note server; context = "none", notes = "read" lets the agent retrieve notes through tools. Neither setting removes earlier conversation history; use /clear to start fresh.

Without [mcp] enabled = true, requests run with no note tools. To use those tools, install the slate terminal executable alongside the desktop app or put it on PATH. Slate checks beside its running executable first, then falls back to slate on PATH. The MCP server reads the same native Slate config and database. No MCP configuration needs to be added to the agent CLI: Slate generates it for each request. Custom commands must explicitly consume that generated config.

docs.title: 4. Check executable discovery and send a request
docs.text:
On Linux/macOS, command -v claude, command -v codex, and command -v slate show the executable paths. On Windows, use where.exe claude, where.exe codex, and where.exe slate (subject to the native Windows limitations below).

Slate inherits the environment of the process that launched it. Shell aliases and functions are not executable commands. If Ask reports cannot start, launch slate-gui from the terminal where the CLI works, or put the actual executable's directory on the desktop session's PATH. Finder and other desktop launchers can have a different PATH from your shell. A custom preset can use an absolute executable path; switching to custom also makes you responsible for CLI flags and MCP integration. argv does not expand ~, environment variables, pipes or shell code.

Open an ordinary, unencrypted note and run :ask Say hello. For a note-access check, use notes = "read" and ask it to read the current note with the Slate tool. Check the returned answer, not just whether the agent process started. The config reloads on every request, so changing the preset needs no restart.

docs.title: Platform status
docs.text:
Platform Slate Ask status Linux Tested with isolated custom-agent/MCP and GUI/terminal checks. Built-in preset qualifications are listed under tool access below. macOS Uses the same Unix process-group runner as Linux, but native builds and agent interaction are not qualified. Check desktop PATH, authentication, and the installed MCP executable on the target Mac. Native Windows Not fully qualified. Sibling MCP lookup currently checks slate, not slate.exe, so PATH fallback may be needed. Cancellation kills the immediate child rather than the entire agent/MCP process tree. Do not treat descendant cleanup as guaranteed.

A vendor CLI supporting an OS does not establish that Slate's integration has been tested on that OS. These limits describe the current implementation; this setup does not change platform support.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
Key / command Action :ask <prompt> Ask; the view opens while the agent works :ask Open the existing conversation and follow-up prompt /clear (in the prompt), or :ask /clear Clear the conversation locally Clear context (desktop button) Clear the conversation locally Shift+Enter Add a line break while typing the prompt Esc Cancel a running request, or close the view Enter Send the desktop prompt; insert the answer from the terminal result view Insert latest / Copy latest (desktop buttons) Insert or copy the latest answer Stop (desktop button) Cancel the run and keep the conversation open ArrowUp / ArrowDown (terminal), wheel / scrollbar (desktop) Scroll the conversation / (terminal result view) Open a follow-up prompt

In the desktop app the input remains available while a reply is running, so you can draft the next prompt. Send it after the current request finishes.

Long prompts wrap in both apps; pasted line breaks are preserved. In the desktop app, click the close button or press Esc to cancel or close Ask; clicking outside the dialog keeps it open.

Agents usually take 10–60 seconds. The terminal shows elapsed time; the desktop shows the running request. The note cannot be edited through the Ask dialog while the agent runs. One request runs at a time: a new one is refused until the previous one has stopped.

The open note is saved before the agent starts. If that save fails (for example because the note changed elsewhere), nothing is sent. :ask is refused for a locked note and for an encrypted one, even when it is unlocked.

docs.title: Conversation context
docs.text:
Closing Ask, inserting a reply, or switching notes keeps the conversation. Each successful exchange retains the prompt, supplied note context, note identity, and answer. Follow-ups send those exchanges together with the current prompt and fresh context chosen by [agent] context. Earlier note contexts are snapshots; a context unchanged since the previous exchange is kept once, not repeated per turn. Failed or cancelled requests are not added; completed note writes still remain.

Type /clear in the prompt or click Clear context in the desktop header to start over. This does not edit notes or contact the agent. History is held in memory for the current app window and is lost on exit. It retains prompts and answers rather than the CLI's internal tool trace. An oversized conversation asks you to clear it instead of silently forgetting older exchanges.

docs.title: What is sent, and what the agent can reach
docs.text:
Everything in the prompt goes to the agent's model provider. The prompt holds:

  • your prompt text and retained conversation history;
  • the context [agent] context selects: the selection when there is one ("selection"), the whole open note ("note"), or nothing ("none");
  • the open note's id and title.

Whatever the agent reads through the note tools is sent to the model as well.

Note access is set by [agent] notes and enforced by Slate's own server, which Slate starts for the request in that mode:

notes The agent can "write" Read, search, create, edit, rename and archive notes and manage collections. Never delete, whatever [mcp] allow_delete says "read" List, search and read notes "none" Nothing: no Slate server is started

Encrypted notes stay unreachable in every mode, as for any MCP client.

The built-in presets also narrow the agent itself:

  • claude runs with no built-in tools (no file access, shell or web), none of your other MCP servers, and none of your Claude Code settings or hooks. Only the Slate note tools for the chosen mode are allowed. Checked against Claude Code 2.1.322.
  • codex runs without your Codex configuration and MCP servers, in its read-only sandbox, with its shell tools switched off. These flags are accepted by Codex 0.167.1, but their effect has not been confirmed by a real run yet: until it is, assume the Codex preset may read any file you can. Codex 0.167.1 also still reads ~/.codex/hooks.json with these flags.

Slate does not sandbox the agent process: it runs as you, in an empty temporary directory so it picks up no project instructions (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md). What keeps a preset away from your files is that agent's own options above.

docs.title: Edits the agent makes
docs.text:
Agent writes go through the same revision-checked saves as any MCP client and are recorded in note history.

While the agent runs, Slate does not reload the open note. When the agent's processes have stopped, whether it finished, failed or was cancelled, its writes to the open note come into the editor as one undo step, and the view says the agent changed this note (u undoes). Inserting the answer afterwards is a separate undo step.

Writes the agent completed before a cancel or a failure stay. If you switched to another note meanwhile, nothing is applied to that note; the writes are stored and :history can bring the earlier version back, as for edits to other notes.

Quitting Slate cancels a running agent first and waits up to five seconds for it. Unix kills the process group; native Windows descendant cleanup remains incomplete (see platform status).

docs.title: Custom agents
docs.text:
preset = "custom" runs a command that implements the stdin/stdout contract:

[agent]
enabled = true
preset = "custom"
argv = ["/absolute/path/to/my-agent", "run"]

The command runs as given, without a shell, with:

  • the prompt on standard input, and its answer expected on standard output;
  • an empty temporary working directory;
  • SLATE_AGENT_MCP_CONFIG: the path of a JSON file ({"mcpServers": {...}}) naming Slate's server in the mode notes asks for, or no server for "none".

Slate gives no guarantee about a custom command's own tools: it is a trusted executable with your permissions. Note access still goes through Slate's server only if the command uses that file. scripts/fake_agent.py is a small working example that reads the file and talks to the server.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom What to check Agent is off Set [agent] enabled = true in the config path shown in the error. Cannot start claude, codex, or custom executable Check the actual executable, permissions, and the environment/PATH of Slate's launcher; use absolute paths for custom commands. Agent exits with a login/authentication error Sign in from a terminal as the same OS user, then retry. Unknown flag Compare the installed CLI version with the preset flags in crates/app-core/src/agent.rs. CLI releases can change compatibility; do not remove isolation flags blindly. No note tools / MCP server failed Enable [mcp], verify the terminal slate executable is discoverable, and check its version and config path. Agent has no selection context Select text before opening Ask, or choose context = "note". The default "selection" sends nothing when no selection exists. Old note details still appear after changing context Conversation history is separate; clear it with /clear or Clear context. Conversation is full Use /clear; Slate refuses an oversized context instead of silently dropping older exchanges. Timed out / no answer Check CLI authentication and stdout behavior; a successful custom command must print nonempty answer text. Increase timeout_seconds only within 1..3600.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• No streaming: the answer appears when the agent is done.
  • Output over 4 MiB, or a run longer than timeout_seconds (1–3600), is stopped with an error.
  • File-backed notes (slate <file>) can be the context, but the note tools cannot reach them.

docs.text:
Command Aliases Purpose format fmt Format markdown document format bold bold Toggle ** around selection format italic italic Toggle * around selection format strike strike, strikethrough Toggle ~~ around selection format code icode, inline-code Toggle ` around selection format clear clear-format, unformat, plain Strip inline formatting from selection format heading-1 title, h1, heading 1, format title, format h1, format heading Convert selected lines to a heading format heading-2 h2, heading 2, format h2 Convert selected lines to a level 2 heading format heading-3 h3, heading 3, format h3 Convert selected lines to a level 3 heading format text normal text, format normal Remove heading and list markers from selected lines checklist toggle toggle, check, tick Tick or untick the checkboxes on selected lines format checklist clist, checklist, checkbox, checkboxes, todo, format clist Convert selected lines to a checklist format unordered-list ulist, unordered-list, unordered, format bulleted-list, format unordered, format ulist Convert selected lines to an unordered list format ordered-list olist, ordered-list, ordered, format ordered, format olist Convert selected lines to an ordered list

Suggestions show only the canonical format names. Abbreviated aliases such as h2, clist, and olist still work. The paragraph command family has been removed; use format in commands and saved keybindings.

In Vim Visual (v) or Visual Line (V) mode, press : and type format to select formatting with Tab completion. Inline styles apply to the selected text; format ordered-list, format unordered-list (also format bulleted-list), and format checklist convert the selected lines. This works in the terminal and desktop apps. With Markdown autoformat enabled, Enter within list item content splits it into two list items, preserving indentation and updating ordered numbering. Enter on an empty item exits the list.

See Diagrams for the block format and canvas controls.

docs.text: Command Aliases Purpose ask [prompt] Ask the local agent, or open the prompt; needs [agent] enabled = true. See Ask the Agent

docs.title: Note organization
docs.text:
Command Purpose organize / tag Open the current note's tag/collection organizer tag add [name] Add one tag, or open the organizer without a name tag remove [name] Remove one tag, or open the organizer without a name note pin / note unpin Set the current stored note's list pin without changing text

Pins respect search and scope filters. File-backed notes do not have stored note tags or list pins. Collection commands below change membership or the working collection; these are separate contexts.

docs.title: Note security
docs.text:
Command Aliases Purpose note encrypt note-encrypt, encrypt-note Encrypt the note with its own password; on an unlocked encrypted note, change its password note decrypt note-decrypt, decrypt-note Store the note unencrypted (a note that left an encrypted collection takes the collection's password)

Both ask for the password in a masked dialog (encrypting asks twice); a password typed on the command line is ignored. Collections are encrypted from the browser (e).

A note in an encrypted collection stays encrypted with the collection's password while it belongs to it: note decrypt is refused, and so is note encrypt for a note the collection's password protects. Remove the note from the collection (:collection leave) or decrypt the whole collection (e in the browser) first.

Without a name, collection join and collection leave open the current note's collection organizer. collection choose without a name opens the working-collection picker. Export suggestions show markdown, pdf and text once each; typing md or txt still matches the full-name suggestion.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Slate reads config from:

  • $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/slate/config.toml
  • fallback: ~/.config/slate/config.toml

The file is auto-generated on first run.

The complete template is config.example.toml, which also supplies the generated file. It lists supported settings and commented script, keybinding and currency examples. Existing files are not automatically rewritten when Slate adds settings.

[editor] command_popup defaults to true and controls contextual suggestions in the GUI, leaving its bottom command bar visible. The TUI always uses the bottom bar with inline word completion and ignores this setting. An explicit value overrides the desktop's remembered preference. Without one, old gui-settings.json values "command_bar": "bottom" and "command_bar": "popup" are preserved as popup off/on respectively.

docs.text:

animations = true

[gui.dialog_animation]

open_ms = 240
close_ms = 160
distance_px = 24

[theme]
color_scheme = "gruvbox-light"
accent = "auto"
icons = "nerd"
# Desktop fonts; the TUI uses its terminal emulator's font settings.
font = "JetBrains Mono"
font_size = 16
fallback = ["Symbols Nerd Font Mono", "Noto Color Emoji", "Noto Sans CJK JP"]

[editor]
markdown_autoformat = true
checklist_auto_reorder = true
autosave = true
reload_outside_changes = true
format_on_save = false
vim_mode = false
# Keep the bottom command bar and show searchable suggestions above it.
command_popup = true
wrap = true
# Editor line numbers. Unset, they show in the TUI and stay off in the GUI.
# line_numbers = true
status_hints = true
date_format = "%Y-%m-%d"
date_time_format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"
variable_autocomplete_min_chars = 3

[editor.modules]
math = true
table = true

[editor.security]
encrypt_notes = false
password_env = "SLATE_NOTES_PASSWORD"

[special_notes]
email_note_prefix = "inbox-email"

[daily]

template = "# {date}\n\n"

[imap]

port = 993
username = ""
password_env = "SLATE_IMAP_PASSWORD"
folder = "INBOX"
poll_seconds = 60
auto_sync_on_startup = false
initial_sync_max_messages = 200
initial_sync_past_days = 1

[perf]

[web_search]

api_key = ""
search_engine_id = ""
max_results = 10

[terminal]
images = "auto"
image_max_rows = 15
clipboard = "auto"

[mcp]
enabled = false
allow_delete = false

[startup]

background_tasks_enabled = true

# Copy scripts/examples/rates.py to your config directory and set its absolute path.
# [currency]
# argv = ["python3", "/absolute/path/to/slate/scripts/examples/rates.py", "EUR"]
# timeout_seconds = 30

Explicit TUI note-list refreshes and wiki-completion loads always prepare their catalogue on a worker, including when optional startup background tasks are disabled. This setting does not switch catalogue hydration onto the input thread.

docs.title: Desktop animations
docs.text:
[gui] animations defaults to true. Set it to false and restart the GUI to disable all menu and dialog effects. [gui.dialog_animation] configures only dialogs: style accepts "none", "fade", "slide", "fade-slide" (default), or "bounce". Opaque slide and bounce exits disappear at the end of their movement; use fade-slide for a fading exit. Fade changes opacity; slide moves the dialog; fade-slide combines both; bounce adds a positional overshoot without resizing its contents. open_ms defaults to 240, close_ms to 160, and distance_px to 24 logical pixels. Distance applies only to slide, fade-slide and bounce. Only delete confirmations dim the window; their backdrop stays fixed and fades with transition progress in every style. Other dialogs leave the note visible behind a transparent click-catcher. Zero duration skips that direction; durations are capped at 1000 ms and distance at 32 pixels. style = "none" leaves menu opening fades enabled.

Dialog actions run immediately while the old presentation closes. A new dialog replaces any closing presentation. Typing and menu switching remain immediate, and no animation frames are requested at rest. Full-page browser, help and history views stay immediate. The TUI ignores these settings.

docs.title: Currency rates
docs.text:
The repository includes rates.py. Register its absolute path under [currency] to enable currency calculations. The optional last argument chooses the base currency (EUR in the example); timeout_seconds defaults to 30 and accepts 1–3600.

Slate loads cached rates immediately, fetches once in the background at startup when background_tasks_enabled = true, and refreshes on :currency refresh. See Currency rates for the script protocol and offline example. Paths do not expand ~.

docs.title: Default collection
docs.text:
Set [startup] default_collection = "Work" to start with an existing collection as the working collection. Note browsing and search are scoped to it, and new notes (including slate --new) are created in it. Names use the same case-insensitive matching as collection commands.

An empty or omitted value keeps all notes in scope. A missing collection shows a status message and falls back to all notes; it is not created automatically. The setting does not change which existing note opens at startup: an explicit note or the most recent note still opens as usual. You can change the working collection during the session with :collection choose Work or clear it with :collection choose none. Encrypted collections still require unlocking before new notes can be created in them.
