docs.title: Editor settings
docs.text:
[editor] keys:

  • markdown_autoformat
  • checklist_auto_reorder
  • autosave
  • reload_outside_changes
  • format_on_save
  • vim_mode
  • wrap
  • date_format: daily note titles and the dates of notes older than a week in the browser and switcher
  • date_time_format: date-picker input, previews, inserted dates, reminders, and a note's modified and added times in the browser preview. Both GUI and TUI accept this format, with or without its clock suffix. Date-only insertion uses the date portion of this same pattern; natural input such as in 3 weeks still works.
  • variable_autocomplete_min_chars

Behavior notes:

  • autosave = true enables implicit save flows (idle flush + save on exit/switch).
  • with autosave = false, explicit writes persist body changes. Switching notes or quitting with unsaved changes is refused once (vim's E37); repeating it, :q! or :e! discards them.
  • a failed save (for example a note changed elsewhere) keeps the editor open with the changes; autosave waits for the next edit. :w! overwrites, :e! reloads.
  • reload_outside_changes = true (default) checks the open note about once a second while idle (in the terminal app also as soon as the terminal regains focus) and loads changes made elsewhere (slate mcp, slate append, slate capture, IMAP sync, another Slate) as one undoable edit when there are no unsaved changes. Set it to false to skip the check; such changes then show up as a save conflict, as before.
  • format_on_save = true runs format before save.
  • vim_mode = true starts the editor in vim normal mode.
  • wrap = true (default) soft-wraps long lines at word boundaries. Tables, code fences, code blocks, and code files keep horizontal scrolling so columns stay aligned. With wrap = false every line scrolls horizontally.
  • line_numbers is unset by default: the TUI shows line numbers and the GUI hides them. Set it to true or false to choose for both; GUI fold controls remain available, and View › Line numbers in the GUI overrides it. Restart Slate after changing it.
  • status_hints = true (default) shows key hints in the terminal status bar: : commands, ? keys, Ctrl+P notes and F1 help in vim mode (Ctrl+E for commands otherwise). Status messages replace them while they show. Set it to false to hide them.
  • variable_autocomplete_min_chars is clamped to 1..8.

docs.title: Per-note module defaults
docs.text:
[editor.modules] sets defaults for new notes:

  • math
  • table
  • variables
  • style
  • cross_note

Module state is then persisted per note and can diverge note-by-note.

docs.title: Note security defaults
docs.text:
[editor.security] keys:

  • encrypt_notes: whether newly created notes default to encrypted-at-rest storage
  • password_env: environment variable name used for default encryption password

Behavior notes:

  • if encrypt_notes = true, password_env must resolve to a non-empty environment variable at runtime
  • a new note in an encrypted working collection is encrypted with the collection's key instead
  • note encrypt/decrypt commands are not supported for file-backed markdown notes (slate path/to/file.md)

docs.title: Daily notes
docs.text:
[daily] keys:

  • note_prefix (default daily): daily note ids are <prefix>-YYYY-MM-DD
  • template (default "# {date}\n\n"): body of a new daily note; {date} uses [editor] date_format

Daily notes are opened with :today or slate today, and slate capture <text> (or piped stdin) appends a - HH:MM text entry without opening the editor.

docs.title: Special notes
docs.text:
[special_notes] keys:

  • email_note_prefix
  • email_rotation (currently daily-local)

docs.title: IMAP
docs.text:
[imap] keys:

  • connection: host, port, username, password_env, folder
  • polling: poll_seconds, auto_sync_on_startup
  • bootstrap and limits:
  • initial_sync_max_messages
  • initial_sync_past_days
  • max_message_bytes
  • max_body_bytes

Runtime validation constraints:

  • poll_seconds: 10..86400
  • initial_sync_max_messages: 1..100000
  • initial_sync_past_days: 0..3650
  • max_body_bytes <= max_message_bytes
  • host, username, password_env, and folder must be non-empty

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
[mcp] keys:

  • enabled (default false): lets slate mcp serve notes to MCP clients such as AI assistants. While it is false, slate mcp refuses to start.
  • allow_delete (default false): also offers delete_note, which deletes a note and its history for good. Without it, clients can only move notes to the Archive collection.

Notes created over MCP use [editor.modules] and [editor.security] like notes created in the editor. See MCP Server for client setup.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
[agent] keys, for :ask (see Ask the Agent):

  • enabled (default false): lets :ask run the agent. The prompt, the context and whatever the agent reads go to that agent's model.
  • preset (default "claude"): "claude", "codex", or "custom" with argv.
  • argv: the command for preset = "custom"; not allowed with the other presets.
  • context (default "selection"): what of the open note goes into the prompt: "selection", "note" or "none".
  • notes (default "write"): what the agent may do with notes through Slate's MCP server: "write" (never delete), "read" or "none". Needs [mcp] enabled = true; without it requests run as "none".
  • timeout_seconds (default 300, 1–3600).

An unknown key or a bad combination is an error shown when :ask runs. Settings reload for every request. Built-in presets resolve claude/codex from Slate's inherited PATH; authenticate the CLI first. There is no Slate model/API-key or extra-arguments setting. A custom preset may use an absolute executable path, but must implement the prompt-on-stdin/answer-on-stdout contract and its own MCP setup. See the setup guide for native config paths, executable discovery, platform qualification, and troubleshooting.

Ask retains one conversation across notes until /clear, Clear context, or app exit. Changing context or notes does not erase earlier exchanges.

docs.title: Date format tokens
docs.text:
Common supported tokens:

  • %Y, %y
  • %m, %d
  • %b, %B

docs.title: Desktop fonts
docs.text:
[theme] font selects the desktop font family throughout the app, and font_size sets its initial size in pixels (9–32). These settings override the remembered desktop size at startup; zoom shortcuts still work during the session. Family names are case insensitive; the old jetbrains-mono spelling also resolves to JetBrains Mono.

fallback lists the installed families available for missing glyphs. All variants of the selected families are retained. A missing configured family is a startup error. With no list (or an empty one), Slate selects a small installed set covering symbols, emoji, and CJK where available. With no primary font, Slate retains separate automatic monospace/editor and sans/UI choices.

On Linux, Fontconfig's cached catalogue resolves the families before GPUI starts. A private font directory restricts discovery to the selected files; other installed families are not parsed. fc-list from the fontconfig package is required. Other desktop platforms use their native font systems; font discovery is not restricted there.

The TUI does not load, select, or restrict font files. Configure its terminal emulator (Ghostty, Alacritty, etc.) for the same primary and fallback fonts.

docs.title: Export Reference
docs.text: Slate supports clipboard and file export from the command bar. It also supports full database backup and restore commands for moving all notes together.

docs.title: Export formats
docs.text:
• markdown (.md)
  • plain text (.txt)
  • PDF (.pdf)

docs.title: Command syntax
docs.text:
• export pdf <path>
  • export markdown [path]
  • export text [path]
  • backup export <path.zip>
  • backup export md <directory>
  • backup load <backup.zip|notes.zip|notes-directory>
  • backup <path.zip> (legacy alias for backup export)
  • backup notes <path.zip> (legacy alias for backup export)

Suggestions display only markdown, pdf and text. The aliases md and txt remain accepted and match their full-name suggestions when typed.

If path is omitted:

  • Markdown and text copy to the clipboard.
  • The desktop app opens a path prompt for PDF; the terminal requires a path and reports usage when it is missing.

Markdown and text currently write the stored Markdown text, with generated TOC fences removed by the shared export preparation. Text export does not strip all Markdown formatting. PDF typesets that content.

Path behavior:

  • ~ / ~/... is expanded to $HOME in command-path exports
  • relative paths are resolved from the current process working directory
  • parent directory must already exist and be writable

docs.title: Export entry points
docs.text:
• command bar export via export ...
  • clipboard fallback for export markdown / export text with no path

docs.title: PDF rendering details
docs.text:
PDF export is markdown-aware and currently includes:

  • headings and paragraph flow
  • ordered/unordered lists
  • checklist rendering
  • fenced/inline code styling
  • generated toc sections as formatted heading lists, preserving nested indentation
  • markdown tables
  • markdown images (![alt](src))
  • diagram fences drawn as vector graphics with real text

Diagrams are drawn from the same shapes as SVG export, at one point per diagram unit, shrunk to fit the page, with a subtle gray frame. They stay sharp at any zoom and their labels are selectable text; opacity, dashes and clipping carry over. Invalid, unfinished, or oversized diagrams retain their source with a “Diagram unavailable” notice. Image budgets (decoded pixels and encoded bytes) apply to note images. Markdown exports keep the editable diagram fences unchanged.

Closed toc fences are omitted from all export formats, leaving their stored Markdown contents. Ordinary code fences, including examples containing a toc fence, retain code styling. Export uses the existing TOC text; run :toc refresh before exporting to update it.

PDF links are clickable: TOC and same-note heading links jump to their heading, and Markdown URL, email, and file links open their destinations. Relative file links are written as absolute file: links, resolved against the note's folder (the app data folder for notes stored in the database), so they keep working wherever the PDF is saved. Bare web URLs and email addresses are linked too. Wrapped labels keep a clickable area on each line, including links in tables and quotes. Links to missing headings stay inactive; refresh a stale TOC before export. Cross-note wiki links are not exported as navigation links.

Color behavior follows export palette rules used by host runtime.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text: Standard PDF fonts declare WinAnsi encoding. On supported installations, the Unicode fallback embeds regular and available sibling bold/italic faces and uses their glyph widths for layout. Only used faces are embedded. Set SLATE_PDF_UNICODE_FONT to a TrueType font file to override the regular face; styled siblings are discovered by family/style filename. A missing styled face uses the regular face; characters absent from installed fonts may still fall back. Font availability therefore affects coverage and styling.

docs.title: Image sources
docs.text:
Image resolution supports:

  • db-backed image placeholders resolved through note source service
  • file-backed markdown image paths
  • data-url image payloads

docs.title: Error behavior
docs.text:
Typical export error classes:

  • invalid/missing path for file export
  • filesystem write failures
  • unsupported/bad image payload during PDF decode
  • clipboard write failure for clipboard exports

Host command status messages are returned to the status bar/toast layer.

docs.title: Database Backup
docs.text:
backup export <path.zip> writes a portable zip containing:

  • notes.db: a consistent SQLite snapshot of the full Slate notes database
  • manifest.json: backup metadata
  • README.txt: manual restore notes

The zip uses stored (uncompressed) entries so the file can be opened by any standard zip tool.

docs.title: Database Restore
docs.text:
backup load <path> automatically recognizes a Slate database backup, a ZIP of Markdown notes (stored or Deflate-compressed), or a Markdown directory. Native backups follow the replacement workflow below. Markdown is added as described in Markdown directory backups: existing notes identified by slate-id retain their edits; files without an id become new notes. Other compressed archive formats are not supported.

A typed directory must look like a note folder: it holds the .slate-export marker written by backup export md, a .obsidian folder, or a Markdown file at its top level. So a slip such as backup load ~ is refused rather than importing every Markdown file below it. A ZIP needs a Markdown file anywhere. A ZIP's single enclosing folder is removed only when it holds the marker or .obsidian; any other single folder may be the content, so it is kept and becomes a collection for notes without collections front matter.

Markdown ZIPs are unpacked to a private folder beside the database (not a RAM-backed /tmp), which is removed after import or failure. Unsafe paths, symlinks and duplicate paths (a.md and ./a.md) are rejected before importing any notes; names differing only by case are distinct files, unless the file system cannot hold both. Extraction is limited to 100,000 entries, 512 MiB per file and 4 GiB total. A ZIP containing root-level notes.db is always treated as a native backup; a damaged backup does not fall back to importing unrelated Markdown files.

For a Slate backup, backup load <path.zip> validates and restores while the app remains open:

  1. Extract and stage notes.db at <data_dir>/notes.db.staged-restore.
  2. Validate SQLite integrity, the schema version, and required tables/columns. Backups at the current schema (1) are restored, older released ones are upgraded first, and pre-release (2 to 6) or newer ones are refused.
  3. Drain in-flight database work and save pending edits before the swap.
  4. Replace/reopen the database, retain the previous file as notes.db.before-restore, and reload note/catalogue state. A failed reopen restores the prior database.

A staged restore left by an interrupted session can also be applied during startup. Normal successful restore does not require quitting/restarting.

Manual restore remains possible: close all Slate clients, unzip a compatible backup and replace the active database. Keep a copy of the original database.

docs.title: Markdown directory backups
docs.text:
backup export md <directory> writes every readable note to a new or empty directory, in the background with its count in the status bar. It refuses a directory holding anything but .obsidian, so it cannot overwrite earlier notes. Directories read like other paths: quotes, a leading ~ and file:// all work. The result also opens as an Obsidian vault.

  • One folder per collection; empty collections get an empty folder. A note in several collections is written once, to the first collection by case-insensitive name, then exact name and id. Notes without a collection stay at the root. Sanitized folder names receive numeric suffixes on collision.
  • Each note becomes <title>.md. Characters unsafe in a file name become spaces, and repeated titles get a number.
  • [[id]] links become [[folder/title]], keeping any #heading and |text. Links in code stay as written, and links to missing notes stay as ids.
  • Front matter holds slate-id, aliases when the name differs from the title, tags, and every collection in collections. Tag spaces become -, and slate-tags keeps the exact names.
  • Stored images go to attachments/, linked relatively from collection folders. Encrypted notes are skipped and counted.
  • An empty .slate-export file marks the directory for backup load.

This is a Markdown export, not a full database snapshot. backup load adds such a directory, or a ZIP of it, back. It reads .md files and skips hidden folders such as .obsidian and .trash:

  • A note whose slate-id already exists here is left as it is, so loading twice adds nothing and never overwrites an edit.
  • The file name becomes a # heading when a file does not open with one.
  • [[name]], [[folder/name]], aliases and relative [text](file.md) links become note links. Links nothing matches stay as text and are counted.
  • ![[image.png]] and relative ![alt](image.png) import the image. Embedding a note, ![[note]], becomes a plain link.
  • Front matter tags and inline #tags become tags; collections, or else the note's folder, becomes a collection (Projects - Deep for Projects/Deep). Other front matter stays visible in a yaml block under the title.

File dates are not kept: imported notes count as written at import.

backup export <path.zip> continues to produce the full database backup described above, with the same archive layout and overwrite behavior.

docs.title: Diagram captions
docs.text:
Add plain text after the opening fence language, for example ```diagram System overview. It appears as a centered caption below the inline diagram and in PDF exports, including source fallback. Captions wrap within the preview width and add no source line or separate line number. Markdown keeps the opening fence; standalone SVG and PNG images omit captions.

PDF export runs in the background in both frontends. In the terminal, editing can continue while the captured note is exported; the status reports completion or failure. Only one PDF export or backup job runs at a time. PNG diagram exports (desktop only) load system fallback fonts only when labels need glyphs absent from the regular export font.

PNG export is the slate-export crate's raster feature, which only the desktop app enables; the terminal app carries no rasteriser. Its tests run with cargo test -p slate-export --features raster.

docs.title: Feature Guide
docs.text:
Every Slate feature in one place, grouped by area, with the keys and commands that drive it.

Conventions:

  • Insert is the text-editing mode (also the only mode when you never press Esc). Normal is vim normal mode.
  • Commands are typed in the bottom bar: : in Normal/Visual, Ctrl+E in Insert or Normal. F1 provides command and keyboard discovery.
  • TUI: commands stay in the bottom bar, with bracketed word completions such as :export [md pdf txt]. Tab/Shift+Tab select completions; Enter or Ctrl+Left fills the selected word, then a later Enter executes. Otherwise Ctrl+Left/Right move by word. Up/Down recall history, and Esc closes the bar immediately. F1 opens the command catalogue.
  • GUI: a compact popup shows up to six recent or contextual suggestions. The bar shows only typed text and a faint completion suffix. Nothing is highlighted automatically. Down or Tab selects; Enter or Ctrl+Left fills the selection, then a later Enter executes. Up recalls history when no suggestion is selected. Esc hides suggestions first, then closes the bar. [editor] command_popup = false keeps the quiet bar with Tab word completion.
  • Full alias lists: Command Reference. Key tables by mode: Keymaps.

docs.title: Notes and switching
docs.text:
• Notes live in SQLite (~/.local/share/slate/notes.db, WAL mode). The last-open note is restored on start.
  • A note's title is its first non-empty line (heading markers dropped) until you rename it in the browser (r); a renamed title stays put like a file name, and an empty name makes it follow the first line again. Encrypting a note keeps its title visible.
  • Markdown files open directly: slate path/to/file.md or slate-gui path/to/file.md (.md, .markdown, .mdown, .mkd); edits are saved back to the file.
  • Terminal colors follow TERM/COLORTERM: true color when advertised or when TERM names a truecolor terminal family (kitty, alacritty, foot, wezterm, ghostty, …) whose COLORTERM was dropped by ssh or sudo, otherwise 256 or basic 16 colors. A nonempty NO_COLOR (or TERM=dumb) uses terminal-default colors with monochrome emphasis for highlighted backgrounds. Capability detection happens once at startup.
  • The terminal app names the open note in the terminal's window title (Note - Slate) and puts the terminal's own title back on exit. Encrypted notes show only Slate there, since the title stays visible in tab bars and window lists.

The note switcher and collection picker are popups styled like the collection browser: a search bar over a list with icons, ages or match lines, and key hints at the bottom. One Ctrl+P query searches titles, tags, collections and note text; use contains: for body text. A collection name appears in the title when the search is scoped to one.

Key / command Action Ctrl+N (Insert, switcher) New note (in the working collection, if one is set) Ctrl+P Search notes with one structured query Tab in the switcher Accept a field or value completion, if available; otherwise move to the results Enter in the switcher In the query, move to the results with the best match picked; in the results, open the picked note at the matching line Up / Down in the switcher query Recall earlier searches; Down past the newest moves to the results Ctrl+L in the switcher Toggle between the working collection and all notes Ctrl+R in the switcher History of the selected note Delete in the switcher Delete the selected note (confirm with y/Enter; protected notes ask for the password) Ctrl+W, Ctrl+Backspace in the switcher Delete the last word of the query Esc / Ctrl+P in the switcher Close it Ctrl+Q Quit (from any mode) F1, :help (:h), ? (Normal) Help: keyboard shortcuts with how each works, then every command; type to filter, Enter puts a command in the command bar

In either collection browser, press P (Shift+P), or choose Pin note / Pin collection from the actions menu, to toggle a persistent list pin. Matching pinned items appear first in the browsers and pickers; the normal sort or search ranking applies within each group. Use :note pin or :note unpin in the editor to pin or unpin the current stored note without changing its text. Pins never override search, tag or collection filters. Desktop rows show a pin icon; terminal rows show * beside the age or count. “All notes” and “Unsorted” remain navigation entries above collections.

The note switcher, collection picker and collection browser fetch lists in pages of 100 as you navigate. Title filters search the entire scope in the background, including notes and collections outside the loaded pages. Changing the scope, filter or sort starts a fresh list. Browser End and Select All can load all matching pages.

Encrypted notes ask for their password (or their collection's) before opening. Content search only indexes unprotected notes.

docs.title: Background activity
docs.text:
Both apps show background work that lasts longer than a second, such as saving, backups or exchange-rate updates, in the status bar with a small spinner.

Slate opens databases with its current schema, and upgrades ones from an older release after keeping a copy (notes.db.before-upgrade-v<N>). A database or backup from a pre-release version (schemas 2 to 6, Slate 0.8.0 and older) is refused with an error and left untouched. To keep its notes, open it with Slate 0.8.0, run :backup export md <directory>, then :backup load <directory> in this version.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
Key / command Action autosave ([editor] autosave = true, default) Saves after a short idle pause on a background thread, and before switching notes or quitting Ctrl+S Save now (in Insert only while autosave is on; otherwise use :w) :w / :w! Write / force write (overwrites a newer revision on disk) :wq / :wq! Write and quit :q / :q! Quit / quit without saving

[editor] format_on_save = true runs :format before every save. If the note changed elsewhere since it was loaded, a save stops with note changed since last load; use :w! to force save.

While idle (unless [editor] reload_outside_changes = false), Slate checks about once a second whether the open note changed elsewhere (slate mcp, slate append, slate capture, IMAP sync, another Slate, an edited markdown file). Without unsaved changes the new text is loaded in place as one undoable edit, with the cursor and reminders kept on their lines (note changed outside Slate; reloaded (u undoes)). With unsaved changes your text is kept and the status line says so: :e! loads the stored note, :w! keeps your version.

docs.title: Note info
docs.text:
Press F4 in the editor, or run :info, to inspect the current note in either front end. The desktop app also has File → Note info. The dialog shows its title, ID, source, tags, collections, creation and last saved update times, encryption, lock state, and unsaved edits. It fits short content and scrolls long metadata lists; long names wrap in both front ends. Opening it does not save or change the note. File-backed notes use filesystem timestamps; unavailable creation dates show “Unknown”.

Use arrows or Page Up/Down to scroll long lists; Home/End jump to the beginning/end. Escape, Enter, or F4 closes the dialog and preserves the editing mode, cursor and selection. Ctrl+I keeps its existing behavior.

docs.title: Note history
docs.text:
Slate keeps older versions of every stored note. Saves less than five minutes apart form one editing session, and each session keeps the text from before it as a version (a session longer than half an hour is split). Versions are stored as the line changes between them, with an occasional full copy, so a small edit to a large note costs a few bytes; the history of an encrypted note is encrypted with it. File-backed notes (slate file.md) keep no history.

Old versions are thinned out when a new one is added: every version of the last day stays, then the newest of each day for a month, then the newest of each week, up to 500 versions per note.

:history (or :versions), H on a note in the browser, or Ctrl+R in the note switcher opens the history in the browser: the current text first, then each version with its time and the lines its session added and removed. The preview shows what restoring would change (- current lines, + lines of the version), or the version's text.

Key Action j / k, arrows, gg / G, Ctrl+D / Ctrl+U Move between the current text and older versions Tab, t Preview what restoring would change, or the version's full text Enter, l Restore the version (y confirms); the text before it is kept as a version h, -, Esc Back to the notes q, Ctrl+B Close the browser

docs.title: Command line entry points
docs.text:
slate                        open the last note
slate --new | -n             create and open a new note
slate --id <note-id>         open a specific note
slate --list | -l            list notes and exit (works without a TTY)
slate <file.md>              open a markdown file as a note
slate today                  open today's daily note
slate capture [text...]      add a timestamped entry to today's daily note and exit
cmd | slate capture          capture piped stdin
cmd | slate append [--id <note-id>]   append stdin to a note and exit
slate imap-sync              pull new mail once and exit
slate mcp                    serve notes to MCP clients over stdio (needs [mcp] enabled = true)
slate --help | -h

docs.title: Daily notes, capture and pipe append
docs.text:
• Daily notes: slate today or :today (alias :daily) opens today's note, creating it from the [daily] template (note_prefix, default daily; template, default "# {date}\n\n"). The cursor lands at the end, ready to type.
  • Quick capture: slate capture buy milk appends a - HH:MM buy milk line to today's daily note without opening the editor. With no text it reads piped stdin, so any command output can be captured:
slate capture call the bank at 3
git log -1 --oneline | slate capture
  • Pipe append: cmd | slate append appends stdin verbatim to the most recently edited note (email inbox notes are skipped); --id <note-id> picks the target note.
curl -s wttr.in/?format=3 | slate append
make test 2>&1 | slate append --id 01HX4VHR...

docs.title: Editing and markdown helpers
docs.text:
Markdown stays raw text; styling is drawn in place (no preview pane).

  • live styling for headings, quotes, lists, checklists, inline code, code fences, bold/italic/strike, markdown links and wiki links
  • a ---, *** or ___ line is drawn as a full-width divider; the Markdown shows again while the cursor is on it
  • list continuation on Enter (bullets, numbers, checklists)
  • checklists - [ ] / - [x]; a trailing /x toggles an item; with [editor] checklist_auto_reorder = true checked items move below unchecked ones
  • markdown table autoformat and alignment while typing (see Tables)
  • soft wrap for prose ([editor] wrap = true); tables and code keep horizontal scrolling
  • undo/redo with cursor restore
Key Action (Insert) Enter New line / continue list / accept popup selection Tab / Shift+Tab Accept completion, else apply calc result, else next/previous table cell, else indent/outdent list item, else insert two spaces Ctrl+W, Ctrl+Backspace Delete word before the cursor (table-aware) Ctrl+Delete Delete forward (table-aware) Ctrl+ArrowLeft / Ctrl+ArrowRight Previous / next word (previous / next cell in tables) Home / End, PageUp / PageDown Line start / end, page up / down ArrowUp / ArrowDown Move by screen row on wrapped lines; move popup selection when a popup is open Esc Close popup, else switch to Normal mode

Keyboard shortcuts (help)

Yanks are copied to the system clipboard as well as the register.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Macros record Normal-mode actions and Insert-mode typing, and replay them.

Keys Action q{r} Start recording into register r (a-z, 0-9; case-insensitive) q Stop recording (status shows recorded @r (N steps)) @{r} Replay register r {n}@{r} Replay n times (3@a) Esc Cancel a pending q / @ before the register key

Replays are capped at 10,000 steps; a longer replay stops with replay aborted: step budget exceeded.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
In-note search (/ or Ctrl+F) is case-insensitive and highlights every match.

In large notes, previews update after a brief typing pause and matching runs in the background. Enter starts the search immediately; n/N pressed while it is running are applied when the results arrive. Escape cancels the preview and restores the original cursor and scroll position.

Key Action type Jump to the nearest match below the start position Tab / ArrowDown / Ctrl+N Next match Shift+Tab / ArrowUp / Ctrl+P Previous match Enter Keep the position (status shows /query (i/n)) Esc Cancel and restore the original cursor and scroll n / N (Normal) Next / previous match after Enter

Across notes: Ctrl+P with contains: shows matching snippets; see Notes and switching.

docs.title: Queries across notes
docs.text:
The note switcher (Ctrl+P), browser note filter (Ctrl+B) and graph search (/ in the graph) accept the same query syntax. Enter title, text, tag, and collection terms in the same search bar. The graph searches when you press Enter in the terminal and as you type on the desktop. Plain words in the title switcher and browser keep ordered fuzzy title matching: cat dog looks for those letters in order. cat AND dog checks each word independently.

At the end of a note-search input, Ctrl+Right completes a field name or a matching tag or collection name. Typing tag:, #, coll: or collection: opens label suggestions immediately, with no minimum prefix length. Up/Down select a suggestion; Tab or Enter accepts it and quotes spaces automatically. Escape dismisses suggestions before closing the search. The TUI also supports Page Up/Down; the GUI supports scrolling the suggestions. Labels are fetched in pages of 100, with eight visible rows, and typing fetches matches for the new prefix. An exact label leaves Enter available to open a note.

Syntax Example Matches title: title:"daily log" Title contains the phrase, ignoring case tag: or # #work Exact tag name, ignoring case coll: or collection: coll:"Work notes" Exact collection name, ignoring case contains: or text: contains:"release date" Literal phrase in indexed note text AND, OR, NOT, -, parentheses (tag:work OR #home) AND -title:draft Boolean combinations; AND binds tighter than OR

By default, the desktop shows field glyphs and the terminal dims typed field prefixes (tag:, title:, contains:, coll:). Set [search] beautiful = false in config.toml to show the literal query without these decorations in both apps. The query language and results stay the same.

Operator words are case-insensitive, so and, or and not work like their uppercase forms. Spaces between terms mean AND, and redundant whitespace is ignored while evaluating the query. Double quotes keep spaces inside a value; \" and \\ escape a quote and backslash. Multiple tags selected with the browser's T control become tag: terms joined with AND in the effective query. Collection scope still applies alongside the query.

In note lists, bare title matches rank by fuzzy score, contains: matches by full-text relevance, and field-only queries show newer notes first. Graph match cycling follows link degree. contains: reads only unprotected notes; a protected note can still match by its title, tags or collections. Consequently, -contains:secret includes protected notes because their bodies are absent from the index. Parse errors show a position and leave the previous result list visible. Bare words match titles in every search view, including the terminal's Ctrl+P picker, the browser's Ctrl+F view, sidebar search, and MCP search_notes. An unfinished contains:rel matches indexed words beginning with rel; a space or a following query term finishes the word and requires an exact match. In Ctrl+P in both apps, Enter (or Tab without a suggestion) moves from the query to the results with the best match picked, and a second Enter opens it, even while a word is unfinished; Up from the first result, Tab or Esc return to the query, and typing edits it again. In the terminal browser's Ctrl+F view, Enter finishes the word. Quotes (contains:"rel") also require an exact token. Quoted bare text such as "cat dog" matches that literal title phrase, while cat dog keeps ordered fuzzy matching. Snippet and matching-line views include only unprotected notes.

docs.title: Wiki links
docs.text:
Syntax: [[ID]], [[ID#Heading]], [[ID|Title]], [[ID#Heading|Title]]. ID is the exact full target note ID (ULID or daily-YYYY-MM-DD), inserted by autocomplete. IDs are case-sensitive; short prefixes do not resolve. Heading and title do not change target identity.

  • Links render collapsed (title only) until the cursor enters them; broken links render distinctly and resolve when the note appears.
  • Without a custom label, a missing target shows ID (no such note) in both apps, retaining any #Heading before the diagnostic. While note titles are still loading after startup, links show their target without it.
  • Typing [[ auto-closes to [[]] and opens a note picker; typing # inside a link suggests the target note's headings.
Key Action [[ Insert link and open note autocomplete ArrowUp / ArrowDown, Enter / Tab, Esc Pick, accept, cancel a suggestion Ctrl+] (any editing mode), gd (Normal) Open the linked note K (Normal) Toggle a preview popup of the linked note; moving the cursor closes it

Markdown links [text](url) are styled in place.

docs.title: Images and image preview
docs.text:
Syntax: ![alt](./assets/image.png). In the editor an image shows as a compact [image: alt] placeholder; the raw markdown appears while the cursor is inside it.

  • Pasting an image file path imports the image into the note's assets and inserts a relative image link.
  • An image itself on the clipboard (a screenshot tool's copy) never reaches the terminal as a paste: p / P with an empty register import it, as does :paste-image. Reading it needs wl-paste (Wayland) or xclip (X11).
  • The preview opens in a bounded dialog using sixel, kitty or iTerm2 graphics (half-blocks as fallback); decoding happens off the input thread and is cached. Inside tmux, passthrough is used when allow-passthrough is on.
  • Remote (http://...) images are never fetched.
Key Action gx (Normal), Ctrl+O (Insert, vim mode off) Preview the image at the cursor gX (Normal) Open it in the default image viewer o in the preview Open the image in the system viewer Esc in the preview Close it

Config ([terminal]): images = "auto" | "sixel" | "kitty" | "iterm2" | "halfblocks" | "off" (off opens the external viewer directly) and image_max_rows (1-100, default 15).

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
A fenced diagram block describes boxes and connectors, one element per line. It stays plain Markdown text: undo, history, search, sync and export treat it like any other code block.

```diagram
node api rect 0 0 140 60 "API server" fill=#dae8fc stroke=#6c8ebf
node db cylinder 260 0 110 80 "Postgres"
node q rhombus 40 140 120 80 "Cached?"
edge e1 api db "SQL"
edge e2 api q route=orthogonal points=100,120
```
  • node <id> <shape> <x> <y> <w> <h> ["label"] [key=value | flag]...
  • edge <id> <from> <to> ["label"] [key=value | flag]...; each end is a node identifier or a free point @x,y (edge e1 api @300,40)
  • Shapes: rect, rounded, ellipse, rhombus, text, cylinder, callout, hexagon, clipped, triangle, actor, document, cloud, gear, arrow. Other names draw as rect and keep their name.
  • Keys: fill, stroke and text take #rgb, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa (with opacity) or none (no fill, no outline or no label); dashed and dotted select the outline pattern; stroke_width= sets connector and outline thickness from 0.5 to 12 (default 1.5). route=straight|orthogonal|curved; arrow=none|end|both; points=x,y;x,y (waypoints). Unknown keys are kept and ignored.
  • Coordinates are whole numbers within ±1,000,000; sizes are positive. Labels escape \", \\ and \n; size= (6 to 96, default 13), align=left|center|right and valign=top|middle|bottom set size and placement. bold, italic and underline format node and connector labels. text_bg=#RRGGBB[AA] gives labels a background; text_bg=none removes it, including the default on-screen connector label background. A node's label wraps to its width and is cut with … when it does not fit its height.
  • Identifiers ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*) are unique per block and shared by nodes and edges.

Unreadable lines are kept exactly as written and are not drawn; the picture shows how many there are. An edge to a missing node is not drawn; a free end is drawn where it is, and moves with a group move or paste when its edge is selected. A repeated identifier keeps its first definition and makes the block read-only on the canvas until the source is fixed. Blocks over 256 KiB or 2,000 elements show their source with a "too large to draw" note; lines over 4 KiB and labels over 1 KiB are unreadable.

In the desktop app a block away from the cursor is drawn as one picture. With the cursor or a selection in it, the block shows its source with the picture under it, so edits show as they are typed. A folded block shows its opening line. The terminal shows the source.

On desktop, :diagram opens the diagram at the cursor; outside a diagram, it inserts an empty block and opens its canvas. Clicking a picture also opens the canvas. In the terminal, :diagram inserts an empty diagram block; inside an existing block it reports that the canvas is desktop-only and changes nothing:

Input Action Drag a node / several selected nodes Move: snaps to a 10-unit grid and lines up with other shapes' edges and centres, with guides shown; Shift moves freely Arrow keys (Shift: one unit) Nudge the selection by a grid step Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo and redo, one gesture at a time, through the note's history Drag empty space Select with a box (Shift adds to the selection) Shift+click Add or remove an element Ctrl+drag, middle-drag / scroll Pan / zoom (eased unless [gui] animations = false) Drag a port (dots on a hovered node) to another node, or to empty space Connect, or draw a line with a free end Drag an end of the selected edge Attach it to the node it is dropped on, or leave it free Drag a corner of the selected node Resize; a live width × height badge shows diagram units Select an edge, drag its handles Bend through waypoints; double-click a waypoint removes it Shapes panel (left; its header collapses it): click, or drag onto the canvas; r o e d t c; double-click empty space Add rect, rounded, ellipse, rhombus, text, cylinder Lines panel: click, or drag onto the canvas Add a free line (plain, arrow, double arrow, orthogonal, curved, dashed); new connections use the last one picked g or Grid Show or hide the alignment grid Fullscreen icon or F11 Toggle fullscreen; Esc exits fullscreen before closing the canvas Enter, F2 or double-click an element Edit its label in place (Shift+Enter breaks the line; Enter or a click elsewhere keeps, Esc cancels) Properties panel (right) Style: preset fill/line pairs, fill and line colour (the colour picker used by graph groups, with an opacity track; None removes the colour, Theme default resets it), keyboard-editable line width (0.5–12, with half-point steps) beside solid, dashed and dotted previews, and for lines route (straight, elbow, curved) and arrows (none, end, both). Text: keyboard-editable size (6–96 pt; Enter applies, Esc cancels), bold/italic/underline, horizontal and vertical alignment, text and background colour. Choose Background → None to remove connector label boxes. Arrange: X, Y, width and height of one selected shape. Each change, pick or drag is one undo step Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V / Ctrl+D Copy, cut, paste at the pointer, duplicate Ctrl+S Save the note Delete, Backspace, x Delete (a node's edges go with it) f, +, - Fit, zoom in, zoom out Esc Cancel the drag in progress, or close

Fixed connections use from_port=top|right|bottom|left and to_port=top|right|bottom|left. Dragging from or onto a side port fixes the attachment; dropping on a node body uses automatic attachment. Free endpoints ignore port attributes. The Connector properties expose each attached end's Auto or fixed side. Fixed ports follow node movement and resizing.

Arrange provides alignment to selection edges/centres, equal-gap distribution of three or more nodes, and matching width/height to the first selected node. Edges are excluded from arrangement calculations. Click X/Y/Width/Height values to enter whole numbers directly; Enter keeps a valid value, Escape cancels. Invalid values stay open on Enter and are discarded when another gesture starts. Each arrangement is atomic, including range and serialized-size checks.

Create next (Arrange) adds a same-sized, same-styled neighbour with a 40-unit gap in the chosen direction, connects fixed facing ports, and opens its blank label. Creation and connection form one undo step; label editing is separate. Copy style/Paste style apply supported styling to elements of the same kind, without copying geometry, labels, endpoints, waypoints, or unknown attributes. The style clipboard lasts until the canvas closes.

The canvas toolbar's sidebar icons at the left and right independently hide or show their panels, with arrows and hover labels indicating the action. The fullscreen icon beside the right sidebar toggle (or F11) fills the screen; closing the canvas restores the window. Grid and Fit control the view.

Open Export… for background, PNG scale and output actions. Export SVG and Export PNG save standalone images through the native save dialog. Copy PNG places an image on the clipboard, with progress and completion shown at the bottom of the canvas. Choose transparent or white background and PNG scale: 1×, 2×, or 3× (output resolution, not canvas zoom). Export uses the current diagram snapshot, preserving fixed ports, curves, styles and clipped labels; unreadable lines or missing endpoints must be fixed before exporting. The note itself is unchanged.

An exported SVG also carries a draw.io copy of the diagram, so draw.io opens it for editing (File > Open, or name it *.drawio.svg). The copy is one-way and lossy: positions, labels, colours, line styles, ports and waypoints carry over; clipped, document, actor and callout use their nearest draw.io shapes, gear becomes an ellipse, and draw.io redraws curves its own way. Edits made in draw.io do not come back to the note.

PDF export renders diagram blocks as images on white backgrounds. If a block cannot be rendered or exceeds the image budget, the PDF includes its source and an explanation. Markdown export keeps the editable fenced source.

Each finished gesture changes only the lines it touches and is one undo step in the note. A gesture whose block changed meanwhile (moved, edited, or no longer a diagram) is refused and the canvas reloads.

docs.title: Inline calculations
docs.text:
Lines that evaluate show a ghost result on the right; non-math lines stay quiet.

200 * 1.19              → 238
50 kg to lbs            → 110.231 lb
sqrt(144) + 3^2         → 21
  • Arithmetic, percentages, unit conversions and everything fend evaluates.
  • Works on plain lines, list/checklist bodies, and table formula cells.
  • Date-like lines (2026-09-29, 29.09.2026, 09/29/2026) are ignored.
  • Clock times and ranges, see below.
  • Large notes compute only the visible region and fill values in off the input thread.
Key / command Action Tab (Insert) Replace the expression with its result (after any open completion popup) :sum / :avg Sum / average the selection, or the whole note without one

:sum and :avg count each variable, formula and formula cell as its computed value, other table cells as their own expression (units kept), and other text as the numbers in it, skipping list markers. The result is inserted after the selection (at the cursor without one) and copied.

The terminal status bar shows sum, average and count only while text or table cells are selected. These live statistics extract numeric literals, skip list markers and digits belonging to names such as usteda_13, and do not replace the expression-aware :sum / :avg commands. An unindented decimal such as 3434.5 kg is a number, not nested list numbering; nested numbering such as 2.1 is recognized on indented lines.

docs.title: Clock times
docs.text:
09:10-11:45                → 2h 35min
09:10-11:45 + 13:00-17:30  → 7h 5min
11:45 - 09:10              → 2h 35min
09:10 + 2h 30min           → 11:40
9am-5pm - 30min            → 7h 30min
22:00-02:00                → 4h
(17:00 - 09:00) / 3        → 2h 40min
10:30-11:00 standup        → 30min
  • Clock times: 09:10, 9:10:30, 9:10pm / 9:10 pm, 9am (a bare hour needs am/pm attached, so 5 pm stays picometres), 24:00.
  • A range is two clock times joined by - with no spaces; it runs forward, past midnight if it ends before it starts (00:00-24:00 is a whole day). With spaces, - subtracts.
  • Clock time - clock time is a duration and clock time ± duration a clock time; adding, multiplying or dividing clock times gives no result.
  • Results read as 2h 35min and 11:10, so Tab and variables keep them: start := 09:10, lunch := 12:00-12:45, then 17:30 - start - lunch.
  • A clock time on its own (meeting at 10:30) shows no result. Words after a calculation are a label (11:45 - 09:10 work → 2h 35min), but a line with more times or arithmetic after its words shows nothing (9:00-17:00 office, 12:00-12:30 lunch): put each range on its own line. to / in converts a duration as usual: (17:00 - 09:00) to min; a clock time does not convert.
  • A variable holding a clock time or duration is not offered to other notes yet. Durations written directly (lunch := 45min) keep only their number, like other units in variables.
  • :sum / :avg do not add up ranges yet.

docs.title: Variables and cross-note variables
docs.text:
• Assign with name := expression; reference by name anywhere in the note. Names are case-insensitive and may contain spaces.
  • Dependents update as definitions change; conversions store numeric values (len := 3 m to km).
  • gd (Normal) on a variable jumps to its definition (the last assignment, the one in effect). On [[id]].name it opens the other note at that definition.
  • Variable names are highlighted; an autocomplete popup appears after [editor] variable_autocomplete_min_chars (default 3) characters.
  • Another note's variable: [[ID]].name (needs the cross_note module); typing [[ID]]. suggests that note's variables.
Key Action ArrowUp / ArrowDown Move in the variable popup Tab / Enter Accept the suggestion Esc Close the popup

Full rules: Variables Specification.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Markdown tables align as you type, and the cursor moves by cell.

  • Formula cells start with :=: :=sum_col(), :=avg_row() * 2, :=tax_rate * subtotal, :=(1,2) + (2,2) (1-based data-row references). . means the formula's own row or column, with an optional offset: :=(.,2) * (.,3) multiplies two cells of the same row, :=(.-1,.) + (.,4) keeps a running total. Such a formula reads the same in every row. To copy a formula, select cells with Shift+Arrows from it and press Ctrl+D (down) or Ctrl+R (right); in the desktop app you can also drag the dot on the focused cell's corner, as in a spreadsheet. Numbered references move with each copy: :=(4,2)-(3,2) filled one row down becomes :=(5,2)-(4,2); . references are kept as written, and $ pins a number so fills keep it: :=(.,2) * ($1,$4) always reads cell (1,4). A filled date continues as a series, a day per row or column, kept in its own format: 03. November 2026., 2026-11-03, 3.11.2026., 3 Nov 2026 and November 3, 2026 are recognised.
  • Helpers: sum_row(), sum_col(), avg_row(), avg_col(). Typing a helper name in a formula cell (sum, avg_) offers them in the autocomplete popup, with matching variables after.
  • Reference errors render as !ERROR#out_of_bounds, !ERROR#non_numeric, !ERROR#self_reference, !ERROR#cycle.
  • Multiline cells use continuation rows starting with |>.
  • Pasting CSV or TSV (cells copied from a spreadsheet) makes a table, the first row its header: on a blank line in its place, otherwise below the cursor's line; p / P from the system clipboard paste it as whole lines. TSV needs the same number of tabs on every row; CSV (, or ;, "-quoted fields) also needs no space after a delimiter, so prose like Hello, world stays text. Inside a code block or a table, or with the table module off, the paste stays text.
Key (Insert) Action \| Start a row / add a column where applicable Tab / Shift+Tab Next / previous cell Ctrl+ArrowLeft / Ctrl+ArrowRight Previous / next cell ArrowLeft / ArrowRight Move within the cell, then cross into the next ArrowUp / ArrowDown Same column, previous / next row Shift+Enter Split the cell into a \|> continuation row Backspace / Delete Cell-aware delete at cell boundaries Ctrl+Backspace / Ctrl+Delete / Ctrl+W Structural edit: merge cells or delete a column from the header

Vim: di|, ci|, yi|, da| work on cells. Select rows and :sum / :avg to aggregate them.

docs.title: Folding
docs.text:
Fold and unfold the block at the cursor.

Key / command Action za (Normal) Toggle fold at cursor :fold (:zc, :closefold) Fold :unfold (:zo, :openfold) Unfold :fold-toggle (:za) Toggle

docs.title: Dates and reminders
docs.text:
Command Action :date Pick a date and insert it ([editor] date_format; date_time_format with time) :remind (:alarm) Set a reminder on the current line (date + time) :remind toggle Remove the line's reminder, or set one if there is none :today (:daily) Open today's daily note

Date picker: type tomorrow, next friday 10 pm, or in 3 weeks in its input. Left/right arrows move the input caret. Tab switches focus between the input and calendar. With calendar focus, arrows move by day/week, PageUp/PageDown (or Ctrl+ArrowLeft/Ctrl+ArrowRight) by month, Alt+ArrowLeft/Alt+ArrowRight by hour, and Alt+ArrowUp/Alt+ArrowDown by one minute. Ctrl+T toggles time, Enter confirms, and Esc cancels. Typed dates and the calendar share the configured formats.

Reminders show as a ghost on their line and fire a desktop notification (notify-send) when due; setting and removing them is undoable.

docs.title: Lookup
docs.text:
Key / command Action :lookup [query] Open the lookup overlay (runs the query if given) type, Enter Run the search ArrowUp / ArrowDown Select a result Enter on a result Open it in the browser (HTTP(S) only) Shift+Enter on a result Insert it as a markdown link at the cursor Esc Close

Config [web_search]: provider = "auto" | "brave" | "google" | "duckduckgo", api_key, search_engine_id, max_results (1-10). Keyed providers fall back to DuckDuckGo on failure.

docs.title: Ask the agent
docs.text:
Off by default; see Ask the Agent for setup, what is sent and what the agent can reach.

Key / command Action :ask [prompt] Ask the local agent (Claude Code, Codex or a custom command) Esc Cancel a running request, or close Enter Insert the answer at the cursor ArrowUp / ArrowDown Scroll the answer / Ask again

The note is saved first. Edits the agent makes to the open note arrive as one undo step.

docs.title: Clipboard and clip-watch
docs.text:
• Vim yanks and :export markdown / :export text without a path go to the system clipboard (status shows the backend used): through wl-copy, xclip, xsel, pbcopy, clip.exe or tmux, otherwise OSC 52. With [terminal] clipboard = "osc52" copies go only through OSC 52, so the terminal holds them: they outlive slate and work over SSH, but a terminal without OSC 52 support drops them silently.
  • Clipboard text is read natively (Wayland data-control or X11), with the same tools as a fallback.
  • Pasted text is inserted as-is (no autoformat pass).
Command Action :clip-watch on (start) Watch the clipboard and paste each new text at the cursor :clip-watch off (stop) Stop watching :paste-image Paste the image on the clipboard at the cursor

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Collections group notes; the working collection is session-scoped and applies to new notes and the Ctrl+P switcher.

Key / command Action Ctrl+G Collection picker (type to filter, Enter set working collection, Ctrl+E edit, Esc close) :collection create <name> Create :collection choose [name] / choose none / clear Set / clear the working collection; omit the name to open the picker :collection join [name] / leave [name] Add / remove the current note; without a name, open its Organize dialog on collections :collection update <name> Edit name, description and default tags (Tab between fields, Enter save) :collection delete <name> Delete the collection only :collection purge <name> Delete the collection and its notes

docs.title: Collection browser
docs.text:
The browser footer shows only the main actions. Press a for Actions or ? for contextual shortcuts: choose with Up/Down (or j/k), run with Enter, and close with Esc. Existing direct shortcuts still work. The popup follows the focused note or collection, exposes batch actions when notes are selected, and keeps deletion behind its existing confirmation.

Ctrl+B, - in Normal mode, or :browse (:explore, :files) opens a full-screen browser in three columns, like the yazi file manager: collections on the left, the notes of the open collection in the middle and a preview of the hovered note (title, age, collections, tags and the start of the body) on the right. All notes and Unsorted (notes in no collection) sit above the collections. It opens on the working collection with the current note hovered and title search focused. Type to filter immediately, or press Esc to navigate.

Ctrl+F (or Ctrl+/) searches note text inside the open collection. Hits show the line they matched on, the preview scrolls to that line with the search terms highlighted, and Enter opens the note there. Title filtering, text search, and tag filtering use the same bordered input style above the results.

Tags classify notes across collections (for example meeting or idea); collections provide the workspace and defaults for new notes. On the terminal notes list, t edits the hovered note's comma-separated tags: Enter replaces its tags, an empty input removes them all, and Esc cancels. Marked notes are unaffected. Tags are saved immediately as metadata, independently of note text and its undo history. The terminal preview wraps tags across at most three lines, with an additional overflow indicator when needed, while reserving space for the note text.

From the editor, :tag add work and :tag remove work add or remove one tag on the open note (names match in any case; spaces are part of the name, commas are refused). Without a name, both open the note's Organize dialog, as do :tag and :organize, Organize… in the GUI note header, or clicking a tag or the collections label there. The dialog lists the note's tags (or, after Tab, its collections) first and marked, then every other one; typing searches and offers to create a new tag, Enter adds or removes the highlighted row, and Esc returns to the note. File-backed notes have no tags.

T accepts comma-separated exact tags (for example work, urgent), requiring every tag to match (AND). Matching ignores letter case, including Unicode and surrounding spaces; spaces within a tag are preserved. The tag filter combines with the open collection, / title filtering, and Ctrl+F text search. The header shows tags: work AND urgent; an unknown tag gives an empty list. Set an empty tag filter or press Esc after clearing any selection and title filter or leaving text search to clear it. The filter survives changing collections, and resets when the browser closes. Collection counts still show total membership. New notes receive collection default tags, not the active browser filter.

A note can belong to several collections, so notes are copied into collections rather than moved like files: y then p adds a note to another collection, x then p moves it out of the collection it was cut from, and d removes it from the open collection without deleting it. u undoes the last of these.

Key Action j / k, arrows, gg / G, Ctrl+D / Ctrl+U Move o, l, Enter Open the collection or note (asks for the password of a locked note or encrypted collection) h, -, Backspace Back to the collections list / Filter the list (fuzzy); Esc clears it t / T Edit the hovered note's tags / set a single tag filter (empty input clears) Ctrl+F, Ctrl+/ Search note text in the open collection (or the hovered one): type to search, ↑ ↓ / Ctrl+N Ctrl+P move, Enter opens the note at the match, Esc goes back Space / Ctrl+A Mark the note and move down / mark all y / x Yank / cut the marked (or hovered) notes p Paste into the open or hovered collection: copy adds the notes to it, cut moves them d Leave: take the notes out of the open collection (the notes stay) u Undo the last paste or remove D Delete the notes, or the hovered collection (its notes stay); y confirms, and a protected note asks for its password instead n / r New note (in the open collection) or collection / rename the hovered one (a note keeps the name; empty follows its first line) e Encrypt the hovered collection, or decrypt an encrypted one s Sort notes by modification time or title w Make the collection the working collection (All notes clears it) R Reload q, Esc, Ctrl+B Close

Icons use Nerd Font glyphs by default; set [theme] icons = "unicode" or "ascii" for other fonts.

docs.title: Per-note modules
docs.text:
Each note stores its own module switches; [editor.modules] sets defaults for new notes.

Module Controls math Master calc switch table Table formulas variables Variable assignments, references, autocomplete style Markdown styling helpers cross_note [[ID]].name references

Commands: :module status (:modules), :module <name> on|off|toggle (also :module on <name>).

docs.title: Note security
docs.text:
Command Action :note encrypt Encrypt the note with its own password; on an unlocked encrypted note, change its password :note decrypt Store it unencrypted again

Both ask for the password in a masked dialog, and encrypting asks for it twice.

An encrypted note's text and history are sealed with its own random key, and the password only unlocks that key, so changing a password does not rewrite the note. Its title stays visible (encrypting pins it; rename it to something vaguer, or clear it to show "Encrypted note"). Renaming an encrypted note asks for its password first. Opening one asks for the password and keeps it unlocked for 15 minutes of inactivity.

Encrypted collections. e on a collection in the browser encrypts it with a password (asked twice): its notes are encrypted with the collection's key, with their titles pinned, and notes created in it, pasted into it or added with :collection join are encrypted too. Entering the collection or opening any of its notes asks for its password once and unlocks all of them. While a note belongs to the collection it cannot be decrypted on its own or given its own password (:note decrypt and :note encrypt are refused); remove it from the collection or decrypt the collection instead. A note that leaves the collection stays encrypted with the collection's password until the collection is decrypted (e again), and can then also be decrypted or given its own password; a collection that still protects notes cannot be deleted. Notes that were locked, or belong to another encrypted collection, keep their own protection.

Reminder text and images attached to encrypted notes are still stored unencrypted.

[editor.security] encrypt_notes = true encrypts new notes by default using the password in password_env. Not available for file-backed notes.

docs.title: Export and backup
docs.text:
Command Action :export pdf <path> Markdown-aware PDF (headings, lists, code, tables, images, checklists) :export markdown [path] Markdown to a file, or the clipboard without a path :export text [path] Plain text to a file, or the clipboard :backup export <path.zip> Back up the whole notes database (runs in the background) :backup export md <directory> Export Markdown files in collection folders; write each note once :backup load <path> Detect a Slate ZIP backup or a Markdown directory/ZIP; restore or add notes accordingly

Details: Export Reference.

docs.title: IMAP email sync
docs.text:
• slate imap-sync pulls new messages once; [imap] auto_sync_on_startup = true polls in the background while Slate runs.
  • Messages are appended to daily inbox notes (inbox-email-YYYY-MM-DD by default), newest first, with UID checkpoints so nothing is imported twice.
  • First sync only takes recent mail (initial_sync_past_days, default 1). New mail triggers a desktop notification.
  • Any IMAP-over-TLS provider works; the password comes from password_env. Build without IMAP: cargo build -p slate --no-default-features.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text: slate mcp lets AI assistants and bots (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, any MCP client) list, search, read, create and edit notes over stdio. It is off until [mcp] enabled = true. Clients can also rename notes, manage collection membership and archive notes. Writes are checked against the revision the client read, encrypted and file-backed notes stay closed, and deleting is off unless [mcp] allow_delete = true. Setup for each client and the tool list: MCP Server.

docs.title: Themes, wrap and other settings
docs.text:
• [theme] color_scheme (14 schemes, default gruvbox-light) and accent; config changes reload live.
  • [theme.colors] replaces single colours with exact hex, or none for the terminal's own (e.g. a transparent background); see configuration.
  • [editor] wrap, markdown_autoformat, checklist_auto_reorder, autosave, format_on_save, vim_mode, date_format, date_time_format, variable_autocomplete_min_chars.

All keys: Configuration.

docs.title: Table of contents
docs.text:
:toc (or :outline) opens a heading picker for the current note in the terminal and desktop apps. Headings appear in document order, indented by level, with their line numbers. Duplicate titles remain separate; headings inside fenced code blocks are excluded.

Type to filter headings with case-insensitive fuzzy matching. Use Up/Down or Ctrl+N/Ctrl+P to choose, Page Up/Down to move ten headings, and Enter to jump. Left/Right, Home/End, Backspace, and Delete edit the query. Escape closes without moving. The picker starts on the section containing the cursor and reveals enclosing folds when jumping. In the desktop app, click a heading to jump. Opening the picker again reads the current text; it never inserts or changes note content.

docs.title: Generated TOC sections
docs.text:
:toc insert inserts a generated section above the cursor's line, keeping the cursor on the original text. Move outside code blocks, lists, and tables before inserting:

```toc
**Table of contents**

- [Introduction](#introduction)
  - [Setup](#setup)
- [Usage](#usage)
```

The contents render as Markdown in both apps. Headings inside code fences are excluded; duplicate headings receive distinct link anchors. Use gd in Vim mode or Ctrl+] on an entry to jump to its heading, revealing enclosing folds.

:toc refresh regenerates every existing toc section in the current note, replacing only the text between its fences. Each insert or refresh is one undoable change. Heading edits do not update a TOC automatically; refresh when needed. An unchanged refresh does not add an undo entry. To remove a TOC, delete its fenced section.

You can also write a closed, empty toc fence yourself and run :toc refresh. Unfinished TOC fences must be closed first. Ordinary code examples containing a toc fence are left alone. The generated text and fences are saved with the note. Exports unwrap closed TOC fences: PDF shows a formatted heading list, and Markdown/text exports contain the stored TOC body without its fences. Export does not regenerate stale entries; run :toc refresh first when needed.

docs.title: Note graph
docs.text:
:graph shows how notes link to each other through [[id]] wiki links, in the terminal and desktop apps. It fills the view in both apps, hiding the note and editor controls until you close it. It opens on the current note and the notes within two link hops of it, following links in both directions. Links inside code blocks and inline code do not count, and notes that are encrypted contribute no links.

Nodes are laid out by a force simulation: linked notes pull together, unrelated ones push apart. The layout is the same every time for the same links. ◆ marks the centre note, ◉ the selection, and ○ a link to a note that no longer exists. The arrow keys or h/j/k/l move the selection to the nearest node in that direction, and Tab/Shift+Tab step through all nodes. Enter opens the selected note. c (or Space) recentres the graph on it, +/- change the number of hops (1 to 4), and w toggles between the local graph and every note. Neither view limits the number of nodes. Escape closes the view.

The desktop advances graphs of up to 2,000 nodes one layout step per frame on the UI thread; larger graphs animate snapshots from a worker. While dragging a node in a graph with more than 2,000 nodes, only that node moves; settling resumes after release. Smaller graphs keep settling around the pinned node during the drag. The terminal settles graphs of up to 1,000 nodes immediately; larger graphs use a worker and show a loading panel until settled. Closing or rebuilding a view cancels its old layout work. Views with more than 2,000 on-screen nodes omit ordinary labels, keeping the selection's label (and the hovered node's on desktop); zooming into a sparse cluster restores ordinary labels. Only visible background edges count toward drawing budgets, and every visible link touching the focused node is kept. These drawing reductions do not change which notes and links are in the graph or available to navigation and search.

In the terminal, / finds notes in the graph by title: Enter selects the best match, and n/N step through the others. ] and [ zoom in and out, Shift+H/J/K/L pan, and 0 shows the whole graph again; when zoomed in, the view follows the selection.

The link index refreshes in the background each time the graph opens, rescanning only notes edited or renamed since the last time. The first open reads every note once and shows its progress ("Indexing links…") until it finishes; later opens show the graph at once and update it if anything changed.

Note text containing embedded NUL characters is rejected on save because SQLite text operations cannot reliably preserve its search locations. Existing note data is not rewritten.

Search accepts unquoted URLs, times such as 10:30, and ordinary titles such as Re: meeting as bare title terms. Known fields still take precedence (title:10:30); close field-name typos such as titel:daily report an error.

A positive contains: query shows matching body excerpts in paged note lists as well as the matching-snippet view. The browser preview highlights and focuses the body hit. Opening a result with a body hit places the cursor on that source line, in either app. Title-only and metadata-only results keep normal opening behavior.

docs.title: Diagram captions
docs.text: Add plain text after the opening fence language, for example ```diagram System overview. It appears as a centered caption below the inline diagram and in PDF exports, including source fallback. Captions wrap within the preview width and add no source line or separate line number. Markdown keeps the opening fence; standalone SVG and PNG images omit captions.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
slate mcp runs a Model Context Protocol server, so an AI assistant or bot (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, or any MCP client) can find, read, create and edit your notes. It is off by default.

The client starts slate mcp as a child process and talks to it over stdin/stdout. Nothing listens on the network. The server opens the same database as the editor, so you can keep Slate open while the bot works: an open note picks up the bot's changes on its own (see Working alongside the editor).
